Child and Adult Care Food Program (CACFP) National Disqualified List.
OMB Control Number:
0584-0584.
Summary of Collection:
This collection is a reinstatement, without change, of the currently approved collection. Section 243(c) of
Public Law 106-224
, the Agricultural Risk Protection Act of 2000, amended section 17(d)(5) of the Richard B. Russell National School Lunch Act (NSLA) (
42 U.S.C. 1766
(d)(5)(E)(i) and (ii)) by requiring the Department of Agriculture to maintain a list of institutions, day care home providers, and individuals that have been terminated or otherwise disqualified from CACFP participation. The law also requires the Department to make the list available to State agencies for their use in reviewing applications to participate and to sponsoring organizations to ensure that they do not employ as principals any persons who are disqualified from the program. This statutory mandate has been incorporated into § 226.6(c)(7) of the Program regulations. The Food and Nutrition Administration (FNA) is still legally required to collect this data and is thereby continuing to collect in violation of the Paperwork Reduction Act.
Need and Use of the Information:
This is a mandatory information collection that is required under statute. State agencies must provide the information necessary to maintain the National Disqualified List. The State agencies use forms FNS-843 Report of Disqualification from Participation—Institution and Responsible Principals/Individuals and FNS-844 Report of Disqualification from Participation—Individually Disqualified Responsible Principal/Individual or Day Care Home Provider to collect and maintain the disqualification data. These forms are accessed through a web-based National Disqualification List (NDL) system, to collect the contact and disqualification information and reasons on all individuals and institutions that have been disqualified and are therefore ineligible to participate in CACFP. The information is collected from State agencies as the disqualifications occur so that the list is kept current. By maintaining the web-based system, the Department ensures program integrity by making the NDL data available to sponsoring organizations and State agencies so that no one who has been disqualified can participate in CACFP. Without this data collection, State agencies would not be able to prevent individuals and institutions disqualified in other States from reapplying to participate in CACFP.

AGENCY:
Under Secretary of Defense for Research and Engineering, Science, Technology and Innovation Board (STIB), Department of Defense (DoD).
ACTION:
Notice of Federal Advisory Committee meeting.
SUMMARY:
The DoD (referred to herein as “the Department of War” or “DoW”) is publishing this notice to announce that the following Federal Advisory Committee meeting of the STIB will take place.
DATES:
Closed to the public Wednesday, November 4, 2026, from 9:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Eastern time.
ADDRESSES:
The address of the closed meeting is 1400 Defense Pentagon, Washington, DC 20301-1400.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Ms. Elizabeth J. Kowalski, Designated Federal Officer (DFO): (703) 571-0082 (Voice), (Email)
osd.pentagon.ousd-r-e.mbx.stib-office@mail.mil
.
Mailing address is Science, Technology, and Innovation Board, 4800 Mark Center Dr., Suite 15D08, Alexandria, VA 22311. Website:
https://stib.cto.mil/​
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
This meeting is being held under the provisions of
chapter 10 of title 5 United States Code
(U.S.C.) (commonly known as the “Federal Advisory Committee Act” or “FACA”),
5 U.S.C. 552b(c)
; and 41, Code of Federal Regulations CFR 102-3.140 and 102-3.150.
Purpose of the Meetings:
The STIB's mission is to provide independent advice and recommendations on matters supporting DoW's scientific, technological, and innovative enterprises. The objective of the meeting is to obtain, review, and evaluate classified information related to the STIB's mission. The STIB will meet with DoW Leadership to receive classified remarks regarding current and future objectives of the DoW and will meet for plenary sessions where the STIB members will have classified discussions regarding a potential Digital Solutions study and a potential Difficult Target Defeat study that may be tasked
(
printed page 66694)
to the STIB, as well as having a classified discussion regarding other potential topics of study based on the remarks made by leadership during the meeting.
Agenda:
The meeting will begin at 9:00 a.m. on Wednesday, November 4th. Ms. Elizabeth Kowalski, Designated Federal Officer and Dr. Mitch Nikolich, Chair of the STIB, will provide opening remarks and a classified overview of potential topics that are likely to be tasked to the STIB for study. At 9:30 a.m., the Honorable Steve Feinberg, Deputy Secretary of War, will meet with the STIB to provide classified remarks regarding current and future objectives of the Department. Next, from 10:30 a.m. to 11 a.m., the Honorable Michael Duffy will meet with the STIB to provide classified remarks regarding modernization efforts for acquisition and sustainment. The Board will have a break from 11:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m. From 1:00 p.m. to 1:30 p.m., the Honorable Elbridge Colby will meet with the STIB to provide classified remarks regarding National Defense strategy and strategic prioritization. From 1:30 p.m. to 2:00 p.m., Mr. David Lorch will meet with the STIB to provide classified remarks regarding integrating and transitioning advanced technologies. This will be followed by a 15-minute break. From 2:15 p.m. to 4:15 p.m., the Board will meet in plenary session to hold a classified discussion regarding study topics currently under consideration by leadership to task the board and to discuss potential studies based on the remarks made by leadership during the meeting. At 4:15 p.m., Dr. Mitch Nikolich will provide closing remarks. The meeting will adjourn at 4:30 p.m.
Meeting Accessibility:
In accordance with section
5 U.S.C. 1009(d)
and
41 CFR 102-3.155
, the DoW has determined that this STIB meeting will be closed to the public. Specifically, the Under Secretary of War for Research and Engineering, in consultation with the DoW Office of General Counsel, has determined in writing that the meeting will be closed to the public because it will consider matters covered by
5 U.S.C. 552b(c)(1)
. The determination is based on the consideration it is expected that discussions throughout will involve classified matters of national security concern. Such classified material is so intertwined with the unclassified material that it cannot reasonably be segregated into separate discussions without defeating the effectiveness and meaning of the overall meetings. To permit the meeting to be open to the public would preclude discussion of such matters and would greatly diminish the ultimate utility of the STIB's findings and recommendations to the Secretary of War and to the Under Secretary of War for Research and Engineering.
Written Statements:
In accordance with
5 U.S.C. 1009(a)(3)
and
41 CFR 102-3.140
, interested persons may submit a written statement for consideration by the STIB at any time. Individuals submitting a written statement should submit their statement to the STIB DFO at the email address provided above in the
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT
section. If a written statement for consideration at a meeting is not received at least three calendar days prior to the meeting, which is the subject of this notice, then it may not be provided to, or considered by, the STIB until a later date. Please note that all submitted comments and statements will be treated as public documents and will be made available for public inspection.

ACTION:
Rescindment of a system of records notice.
SUMMARY:
In accordance with the Privacy Act of 1974, DFAS is providing notice to rescind a system of records titled “Centralized Travel History Records (CTHR),” T7333a. DFAS established this system to equip Air Force installations with online inquiry capabilities. This functionality allowed installations to support travel claims, questions, and investigations, and to obtain voucher numbers for retrieving travel vouchers from on-site storage or Federal Records Centers. DFAS decommissioned the system and consolidated its records under the Commanders Resource Integration System, F065 AF FMP C.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Background
The DFAS system of records Centralized Travel History Records, (CTHR) T7333a (January 2, 2014;
79 FR 115
) was established to provide Air Force installations with the capability to accomplish an online inquiry to support travel claims, questions, and investigations and provide voucher numbers to retrieve travel vouchers from on-site storage or the Federal Records Centers. The system was decommissioned, and the records are now consolidated under the Commanders Resource Integration System, F065 AF FMP C (December 16, 2010;
75 FR 78684
).
DoD SORNs are published in the
Federal Register
and are available at the Oversight and Compliance Directorate, Privacy and Civil Liberties Division website at
https://doc.defense.gov/​DIRECTORATES/​Privacy-and-Civil-Liberties-Directorate/​Privacy/​SORNs/​
.
II. Privacy Act
Under the Privacy Act, a “system of records” is a group of records under the control of an agency from which information is retrieved by the name of an individual or by some identifying number, symbol, or other identifying particular assigned to the individual. In the Privacy Act, an individual is defined as a U.S. citizen or alien lawfully admitted for permanent residence.
(
printed page 66695)
In accordance with
5 United States Code 552a(r)
and Office of Management and Budget (OMB) Circular No. A-108, DoD has provided a report of this SORN rescindment to OMB and Congress.

EPA will consider the comments received and amend the ICR as appropriate. The final ICR package will then be submitted to OMB for review and approval. At that time, EPA will issue another
Federal Register
notice to announce the submission of the ICR to OMB and the opportunity to submit additional comments to OMB.
Abstract:
This Information Collection Request (ICR) renewal supports activities to implement the National Oil and Hazardous Substances Pollution Contingency Plan (NCP), Subpart J (
40 CFR 300.900
),
Use of Dispersants and Other Chemicals and Biological Agents
. The use of bioremediation agents, dispersants, surface washing agents, solidifiers, herding agents and other substances (
e.g.
sorbents) in response to oil spills in U.S. waters or adjoining shorelines is governed by Subpart J of the NCP regulation (
40 CFR 300.900
). Subpart J requirements include criteria for listing oil spill mitigating agents on the NCP Product Schedule and sorbent products on the Sorbent Product List. EPA's regulation, which is codified at
40 CFR 300.900
, requires that EPA prepare a schedule of “dispersants,
(
printed page 66700)
other chemicals, and other spill mitigating devices and substances, if any, that may be used in carrying out the NCP.” Requirements under Subpart J of the NCP are required by section 311(d)(2)(G) of the Clean Water Act (CWA), as amended by the Oil Pollution Act of 1990. The NCP Product Schedule and Sorbent Product List are used by Federal On-Scene Coordinators (FOSCs), Regional Response Teams (RRTs), and Area Planners to identify spill mitigating agents in preparation for and response to oil spills. Under Subpart J, manufacturers who want to add a product to the NCP Product Schedule or Sorbent Product List must submit technical product data including applicable toxicity and efficacy testing data to the EPA as stipulated in
40 CFR 300.915
. Subpart J requires the manufacturer to submit the corresponding technical product data along with other detailed information to the EPA Office of Resource Conservation and Recovery, Office of Land and Emergency Management. The NCP Product Schedule and Sorbent Product List are available to Federal On-Scene Coordinators (FOSCs), Regional Response Teams (RRTs), and Area Committees for helping them select the most appropriate products to use in various spill scenarios.
In June 2023 EPA promulgated a final rule (
88 FR 38280
, June 12, 2023). This rule revised Subpart J of the NCP by adding new testing and listing criteria for products to be listed on the NCP Product Schedule and establishing the Sorbent Product List. Effective June 10, 2026, only products that are submitted and listed based on the amended testing and listing criteria will be listed on the NCP Product Schedule. All products identified as sorbents prior to the June 2023 rule remained available for use until December 12, 2025, at which time all sorbent products must have submitted information as applicable under the amended testing and listing requirements in June 2023 rule and be listed in the new Sorbent Product List. As of September 2026, the NCP Product Schedule included seven manufacturers and seven products (four dispersants and three surface washing agents). There are currently 12 sorbents listed on the Sorbent Product List. EPA estimates that for each year of this ICR renewal period five manufacturers will apply to list a product on the NCP Product Schedule and 10 manufactures will apply to list a sorbent on the Sorbent Product List. Therefore, over the three-year period covered by this ICR renewal, EPA estimates an additional 15 products may be listed on the NCP Product Schedule, and an additional 30 sorbents may be listed on the Sorbent Product List.
At
40 CFR 300.950
, respondents may claim certain information in the technical product data submissions as proprietary business information (PBI). EPA will handle such claims pursuant to the provisions in
40 CFR part 2, subpart B
. Such information must be submitted separately from non-PBI information, clearly identified, and clearly marked “Proprietary Business Information.” If the applicant fails to make such a claim at the time of submittal, EPA may make the information available to the public without further notice.

There is an increase of 8 hours in the total estimated respondent burden compared with the ICR currently approved by OMB. This is due to changes in testing and listing requirements as a result of the June 2023 rule.

SUMMARY:
In accordance with the Clean Air Act, as amended (CAA or the Act), notice is given of a proposed consent decree in

v.
Zeldin,
No. 3:25-cv-08994-WHO. On October 19, 2025, Plaintiff Our Children's Earth Foundation filed a complaint in the United States District Court for the Northern District of California, San Francisco Division. Plaintiff alleged that the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA or the Agency) failed to perform certain non-discretionary duties in accordance with the Act to timely respond to numerous state implementation plan (SIP) submissions from the State of California. The EPA is providing notice of this proposed consent decree, which would resolve all claims in the case by establishing deadlines for the EPA to take final actions as specified in the decree.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Obtaining a Copy of the Proposed Consent Decree
The official public docket for this action (identified by Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OGC-2026-9077) contains a copy of the proposed consent decree. The official public docket is available for public viewing at the Office of Environmental Information (OEI) Docket in the EPA Docket Center, EPA West, Room 3334, 1301 Constitution Ave. NW, Washington, DC. The EPA Docket Center Public Reading Room is open from 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., Monday through Friday, excluding legal holidays. The telephone number for the Public Reading Room is (202) 566-1744 and the telephone number for the OEI Docket is (202) 566-1752.
The electronic version of the public docket for this action contains a copy of the proposed consent decree and is available through
https://www.regulations.gov
.
You may use
https://www.regulations.gov
to submit or view public comments, access the index listing of the contents of the official public docket, and access those documents in the public docket that are available electronically. Once in the system, key in the appropriate docket identification number then select “search.”
II. Additional Information About the Proposed Consent Decree
The proposed consent decree would establish deadlines for EPA to take action pursuant to CAA section 110(k) on certain SIP submissions by the State of California. Under the terms of the proposed consent decree, EPA shall, in accordance with a stated schedule, take final action in response to all the California SIP submittals identified in the litigation that are still at issue (
i.e.,
that EPA has not otherwise taken action on during the pending litigation). The schedule requires EPA to take such action on a certain specified number of the California SIP submittals that are at issue by each of six successive dates—December 15, 2026, December 15, 2027, December 15, 2028, June 15, 2029, December 15, 2029, and December 15, 2030—such that by the last such date EPA will have taken action on all the submittals. In some instances, the schedule specifically identifies particular SIP submittals in response to which EPA must take action by a specified date, but otherwise, the schedule states that EPA must take action on a minimum number of submittals by each date. It is possible, while this litigation is pending and before the proposed consent decree is final, as EPA continues in the ordinary course of its administrative activities, that EPA may take action on more of the California SIP submittals presently at issue (and which the proposed consent decree currently addresses). In that event, the parties subsequently may slightly adjust the proposed consent decree to ensure that the consent decree is limited to the remaining outstanding SIP submittals. The structure and essence of the proposed consent decree would be unchanged, though, and EPA will be required to take action on all of the remaining SIP submittals at issue in accordance with the prescribed schedule.

AGENCY:
Coast Guard, DHS.
ACTION:
Supplemental notice of proposed rulemaking.
SUMMARY:
The Coast Guard is proposing to alter the operating schedule that governs the Eighth Street Bridge, mile 0.29 and the Tenth Street Bridge, mile 0.43, over the Manitowoc River, in the town of Manitowoc, Wisconsin. The City of Manitowoc has requested a full review of the current bridge regulations to alleviate vehicle congestion in downtown Manitowoc and to operate both bridges remotely. On May 21, 2025, we published an interim rule requesting comments in the
Federal Register
. We are now proposing to include remote operations for the drawbridges. We invite your comments on this proposed rulemaking.
DATES:
Comments and related material must reach the Coast Guard on or before: November 23, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
You may submit comments identified by docket number USCG-2024-0407 at
https://www.regulations.gov
.
See the “Public Participation and Request for Comments” portion of the
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION
section below for instructions on submitting comments. This notice of proposed rulemaking with its plain-language, 100-word-or-less proposed rule summary will be available in this same docket.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
If you have questions on this rule making, call or email Mr. Lee D. Soule, Bridge Management Specialist, Ninth Coast Guard District; telephone 216-902-6085, email
Lee.D.Soule@uscg.mil
.

I. Table of Abbreviations

II. Background, Purpose and Legal Basis
The Eighth Street Bridge, mile 0.29, over the Manitowoc River, is a double leaf bascule bridge that provides a horizontal clearance of 120 feet and a vertical clearance of 12 feet above LWD in the closed position and an unlimited clearance in the open position. The Tenth Street Bridge, mile 0.43, over the Manitowoc River, is a double leaf bascule bridge that provides a horizontal clearance of 120 feet and a vertical clearance of 14 feet above LWD in the closed position and an unlimited clearance in the open position. The Eighth Street Bridge, mile 0.29 and the Tenth Street Bridge, mile 0.43, over the Manitowoc River follow special operations regulations found in
33 CFR 117.1089
.
In an attempt to alleviate traffic congestion in downtown Manitowoc, WI, while serving the reasonable needs of navigation, on May 21, 2025, we published an interim rule to allow the public to test an alternative drawbridge schedule and requested comments in the
Federal Register
(
90 FR 21694
). The interim rule and request for comment did not include remote operations. The city of Manitowoc proposed to operate one of the bridges remotely.
The District Commander has directed a Cybersecurity review of the bridges and found that the owner-provided safeguards appear sufficient for approval for remote operations.
There is a control house at each bridge allowing one drawtender to operate one or both bridges remotely. The bridges will be required to maintain and operate a radiotelephone, and a two-way public address system capable of responding to sound signals or voice communication between the operator and vessels.
III. Discussion of Proposed Rule
The Coast Guard proposes including a provision authorizing remote operations in the regulations governing the Manitowoc Drawbridge Operations. The Coast Guard has reviewed the city of Manitowoc's proposed operating procedures of the bridge and completed a Cyber Security Assessment. There is a control house at each bridge allowing one drawtender to operate one or both bridges remotely. The bridges will be required to maintain and operate a radiotelephone, and a two-way public address system capable of responding to sound signals or voice communication between the operator and vessels.
V. Regulatory Analyses
We developed this proposed rule after considering numerous statutes and Executive Orders related to rulemaking. Below we summarize our analyses based on these statutes and Executive Orders.
A. Impact on Small Entities
The Regulatory Flexibility Act of 1980,
5 U.S.C. 601-612
, as amended, requires federal agencies to consider the potential impact of regulations on small entities during rulemaking. The term “small entities” comprises small businesses, not-for-profit organizations that are independently owned and operated and are not dominant in their fields, and governmental jurisdictions with populations of less than 50,000. The Coast Guard certifies under
5 U.S.C. 605(b)
that this proposed rule would not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities for the following reasons. This regulatory action determination is based on the ability that vessels can still transit the bridge as if a drawtender was in attendance.
If you think that your business, organization, or governmental jurisdiction qualifies as a small entity and that this rule would have a significant economic impact on it, please submit a comment (see
ADDRESSES
) explaining why you think it qualifies and how and to what degree this rule would economically affect it.
(
printed page 66661)
Under section 213(a) of the Small Business Regulatory Enforcement Fairness Act of 1996 (
Pub. L. 104-121
), we want to assist small entities in understanding this proposed rule. If the proposed rule would affect your small business, organization, or governmental jurisdiction and you have questions concerning its provisions or options for compliance, please contact the person listed in the
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT
section. The Coast Guard will not retaliate against small entities that question or complain about this proposed rule or any policy or action of the Coast Guard.
B. Collection of Information
This proposed rule would call for no new collection of information under the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (
44 U.S.C. 3501-3520
.).
C. Federalism and Indian Tribal Government
A rule has implications for federalism under
Executive Order 13132
(Federalism), if it has a substantial direct effect on the States, on the relationship between the national government and the States, or on the distribution of power and responsibilities among the various levels of government. We have analyzed this proposed rule under that Order and have determined that it is consistent with the fundamental federalism principles and preemption requirements described in
Executive Order 13132
.
Also, this proposed rule does not have tribal implications under
Executive Order 13175
(Consultation and Coordination with Indian Tribal Governments) because it would not have a substantial direct effect on one or more Indian tribes, on the relationship between the Federal Government and Indian tribes, or on the distribution of power and responsibilities between the Federal Government and Indian tribes. If you believe this proposed rule has implications for federalism or Indian tribes, please contact the person listed in the
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT
section.
D. Unfunded Mandates Reform Act
The Unfunded Mandates Reform Act of 1995 (
2 U.S.C. 1531-1538
) requires Federal agencies to assess the effects of their discretionary regulatory actions. In particular, the Act addresses actions that may result in the expenditure by a State, local, or tribal government, in the aggregate, or by the private sector of $100,000,000 (adjusted for inflation) or more in any one year. Though this proposed rule will not result in such an expenditure, we do discuss the effects of this proposed rule elsewhere in this preamble.
E. Environment
We have analyzed this rule under Department of Homeland Security Management Directive 023-01, Rev. 1, associated implementing instructions, and Environmental Planning Policy COMDTINST 5090.1 (series), which guide the Coast Guard in complying with the National Environmental Policy Act of 1969 (NEPA)(
42 U.S.C. 4321
et seq.
). The Coast Guard has that this action is one of a category of actions that do not individually or cumulatively have a significant effect on the human environment. This proposed rule promulgates the operating regulations or procedures for drawbridges. Normally such actions are categorically excluded from further review, under paragraph L49, of Appendix A, Table 1 of DHS Instruction Manual 023-01-001-01, Rev. 1.
Neither a Record of Environmental Consideration nor a Memorandum for the Record are required for this rule. We seek any comments or information that may lead to the discovery of a significant environmental impact from this proposed rule.
VI. Public Participation and Request for Comments
We view public participation as essential to effective rulemaking and will consider all comments and material received during the comment period. Your comment can help shape the outcome of this rulemaking. If you submit a comment, please include the docket number for this rulemaking, indicate the specific section of this document to which each comment applies, and provide a reason for each suggestion or recommendation.

https://www.regulations.gov

type USCG-2024-0407 in the search box and click “Search.” Next, look for this document in the Search Results column, and click on it. Then click on the Comment option. If your material cannot be submitted using

Viewing material in docket.
To view documents mentioned in this proposed rule as being available in the docket, find the docket as described in the previous paragraph, and then select “Supporting & Related Material” in the Document Type column. Public comments will also be placed in our online docket and can be viewed by following instructions on the
https://www.regulations.gov

Personal information.
We accept anonymous comments. Comments we post to

AGENCY:
National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS), National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), Commerce.
ACTION:
Inseason modification of 2026-2027 management measures.
SUMMARY:
NMFS announces eleven inseason actions for 2026-2027 ocean salmon fisheries. These inseason actions modified the commercial salmon fisheries in the area from United States/Canada border to Cape Falcon, OR.
DATES:
The effective dates for these inseason actions are set out in this
(
printed page 66656)
document under the heading “Inseason Actions” and the actions remained in effect until superseded or modified.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Shannon Penna, (562) 980-4239,
Shannon.Penna@noaa.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
The annual management measures for the 2026-2027 ocean salmon fisheries (
91 FR 29092
, May 19, 2026) govern the commercial and recreational fisheries in the area from the United States/Canada border to the United States/Mexico border, effective from 0001 hours Pacific Daylight Time (PDT), May 16, 2026, until the effective date of the 2027-2028 management measures, which we expect to be May 16, 2027. NMFS is authorized to implement inseason management actions to modify fishing seasons, catch limits, and other management measures considering factors described in regulation (
50 CFR 660.409
). Inseason actions in the salmon fishery may be taken directly by NMFS (
50 CFR 660.409(a)
—Fixed inseason management provisions) or upon consultation with the Chairman of the Pacific Fishery Management Council (Council), and the appropriate State Directors (
50 CFR 660.409(b)
—Flexible inseason management provisions).
Management of the salmon fisheries is divided into two geographic areas: north of Cape Falcon (NOF) (United States/Canada border to Cape Falcon, OR) and south of Cape Falcon (SOF) (Cape Falcon, OR, to the United States/Mexico border). This notice describes inseason actions taken during the 2026-2027 management cycle. These actions affected the NOF commercial salmon fishery, as set out under the heading Inseason Actions below.
Consultation on these inseason actions took place with the Council salmon staff officer and representatives for the appropriate State Directors on May 18, 2026, May 27, 2026, June 3, 2026, June 11, 2026, June 18, 2026, and June 25, 2026. This consultation also included representatives from NMFS, Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife (WDFW), and Oregon Department of Fish and Wildlife. Representatives from the Salmon Advisory Subpanel and the Salmon Technical Team were also present.
These inseason actions were announced via the NMFS' telephone hotline and U.S. Coast Guard radio broadcast at the time the actions became effective. (
50 CFR 660.411(a)(2)
).
Inseason Actions
Inseason Action #1
Description of the action:
Inseason action #1 modified the commercial salmon troll fishery from the United States/Canada border to Cape Falcon, OR.
Added a landing and possession limit for the entire area between the United States/Canada border and Cape Falcon for 200 Chinook salmon per vessel per landing week (Thursday-Wednesday).
The landing and possession limit in the subareas between the United States/Canada border and the Queets River was 100 Chinook salmon per vessel per landing week (Thursday through Wednesday).
The landing and possession limit for the subarea between the Queets River and Leadbetter Point was 200 Chinook salmon per vessel per landing week (Thursday through Wednesday).
The landing and possession limit in the subarea between Leadbetter Point and Cape Falcon was 80 Chinook salmon per vessel per landing week (Thursday through Wednesday).
Effective dates:
Inseason action #1 went into effect at 12:01 a.m., on May 18, 2026, and remained in effect until 11:59 p.m., May 27, 2026.
Reason and authorization for the action:
Catch rates were lower than anticipated going into the spring season, so increasing the landing and possession limits allowed for more opportunities for fisheries to take advantage of the economic benefit of higher prices early in the season, good fishing, and weather windows. To accomplish this, a landing and possession limit was set for the entire area NOF as well as limits for specific subareas. Fishers were allowed to fish up to the subarea limits in multiple subareas, but not exceed the overall NOF landing and possession limit. One limit for the entire NOF area allows for enhanced ability to manage the quota effectively by avoiding fishers catching the full subarea limit in multiple subareas and preventing much higher cumulative catch early in the season. A limit for the entire NOF area and lower limits in certain subareas also ensures fair fishing opportunity throughout the fishery and across ports. The varying limits throughout the smaller subareas allow for greater access to the quota based on the availability of fish in each subarea, which allows for more equitable fishing opportunity and a longer fishing season.
The Regional Administrator (RA) considered the abundance forecasts for Chinook salmon stocks, the timing of the action relative to the length of the season, catch and effort to date, projected catch and effort under the proposed action, and other relevant factors and determined that the inseason action described above was necessary to meet management and conservation goals set preseason. This inseason action modified species caught and landed during specific seasons and the establishment or modification of limited retention regulations under
50 CFR 660.409(b)(1)(ii)
.
Inseason Action #2
Description of the action:
Inseason action #2 modified the landing and possession limit for the commercial salmon troll fishery in the area between the United States/Canada border and Cape Falcon, OR, from 200 Chinook salmon per vessel per landing week (Thursday through Wednesday) to 100 Chinook salmon per vessel per landing week (Thursday through Wednesday).
Effective dates:
Inseason action #2 went into effect at 12:01 a.m., on May 28, 2026, and remained in effect until 11:59 p.m., June 3, 2026.
Reason and authorization of the action:
Due to high fishing effort and catch rates for the fishing week of May 21, 2026, through May 27, 2026, the overall NOF landing and possession limit was decreased. Chinook salmon catch was 4,422 that week on a spring season quota of 37,300, with 13,481 Chinook salmon remaining on the quota for the season ending the earlier of June 29, 2026, or attainment of the quota. This inseason action was necessary to preserve the quota for the length of the season and keep trip limits at economically viable levels.
The RA considered the abundance forecasts for Chinook salmon stocks, the timing of the action relative to the length of the season, catch and effort to date, projected catch and effort under the proposed action compared with the remaining quota, and other relevant factors and determined that the inseason action described above is necessary to meet management and conservation goals set preseason. This inseason action modified species caught and landed during specific seasons and the establishment or modification of limited retention regulations under
50 CFR 660.409(b)(1)(ii)
.
Inseason Action #3-#5
Description of action #3:
Inseason action #3 modified the landing and possession limit for the commercial salmon troll fishery in the area between the United States/Canada border and Cape Falcon, OR from 100 Chinook salmon per vessel per landing week
(
printed page 66657)
(Thursday through Wednesday) to 50 Chinook salmon per vessel per landing week (Thursday through Wednesday).
Effective dates:
Inseason action #3 went into effect at 12:01 a.m., on June 4, 2026, and remained in effect until 11:59 p.m., on June 9, 2026.
Reason and Authorization of the Action—See Below
Inseason Action #4
Description of action #4:
Inseason action #4 modified the commercial salmon troll fishery. The area between United States/Canada border and Cape Falcon, OR was closed.
Effective dates:
Inseason action #4 went into effect at 11:59 p.m., on June 9, 2026, and remained in effect until 11:59 p.m., June 11, 2026.
Reason and Authorization of the Action—See Below
Inseason Action #5
Description of action #5:
Inseason action #5 modified the ocean salmon troll commercial fishery. The area between the United States/Canada border and Cape Falcon, OR was reopened Fridays through Tuesdays only, closed Wednesdays and Thursdays with a landing and possession limit of 50 Chinook salmon per vessel.
Effective dates:
Inseason action #5 went into effect on June 12, 2026, and remained in effect until June 16, 2026.
Reason and authorization of the actions #3-#5:
Due to good weather and an increase in effort, the catch rate was high for the landing week from May 28, 2026, through June 3, 2026. The Chinook salmon catch that week was 7,300 on a spring season quota of 37,300, with 6,181 Chinook salmon remaining on the quota. To slow down catch and effort to provide opportunity while preserving the length of the season, the landing and possession limit for the entire NOF area was reduced to 50 Chinook salmon per vessel per landing week from 100 Chinook per vessel per landing week (Inseason #3). On June 9, 2026, the fishery was closed to assess landings to determine if there remained sufficient quota to allow for additional fishing opportunity (Inseason #4). After assessing the landings made between June 4, 2026, through June 9, 2026, and the remaining quota, the area NOF reopened with a 50 Chinook salmon landing and possession limit, but with a shorter landing week to access the remaining spring quota while preserving the length of the season (Inseason #5).
The RA considered the quotas for Chinook salmon stocks, the timing of the action relative to the length of the season, catch and effort to date, projected catch and effort under the proposed action, and other relevant factors like weather, and determined that the inseason action described above is necessary to meet management and conservation goals set preseason. Inseason action #4 closed the fishery to assess catch and reassess landing limits for Chinook salmon as they were reaching their quota. These actions were intended to prolong season length and fishing opportunity. With a limited spring quota remaining, inseason action #4 was necessary to ensure that the Chinook salmon quota was not exceeded. Inseason action #4 modified the fishing season consistent with
50 CFR 660.409(b)(1)(i)
. Inseason actions #3 and #5 modified the number of species that may be caught and landed during specific seasons and the establishment or modification of limited retention regulations under
50 CFR 660.409(b)(1)(ii)
.
Inseason Actions #6-#7
Description of action #6:
Inseason action #6 modified the commercial salmon troll fishery in the area between the United States/Canada border and Cape Falcon. The overall NOF landing and possession limit was reduced from 50 Chinook salmon per vessel to 35 Chinook salmon per vessel for the open period.
Effective dates:
Inseason action #6 went into effect at 12:01 a.m., June 12, 2026, and remained in effect until 11:59 p.m., June 16, 2026.
Reason and Authorization of the Action—See Below
Description of action #7:
Inseason action #7 modified the commercial salmon troll fishery. The area between the United States/Canada border and Cape Falcon was closed.
Effective dates:
Inseason action #7 went into effect at 11:59 p.m., on June 16, 2026, and remained in effect until 11:59 p.m., on June 18, 2026.
Reason and Authorization of the Action—See Below
Reason and authorization of inseason actions #6 and #7:
As of June 12, 2026, the Chinook salmon catch was 34,149 on a spring season quota of 37,300 Chinook salmon, with 3,151 quota remaining. To slow down catch and effort to preserve the season length and quota while providing opportunity, the landing and possession limit for the entire NOF area was reduced to 35 Chinook salmon per vessel per landing week from 50 Chinook per vessel per landing week (Action #6). To avoid exceeding the quota and evaluate the week's landings, the fishery closed on June 16, 2026 (Action #7).
The RA considered the quotas for Chinook salmon stocks, the timing of the action relative to the length of the season, catch and effort to date, projected catch and effort under the proposed action, and other relevant factors like weather, and determined that Inseason action #6 was necessary to meet management and conservation goals set preseason. Inseason action #6 modified the number of species that may be caught and landed during specific seasons and the establishment or modification of limited retention regulations under
50 CFR 660.409(b)(1)(ii)
. Inseason action #7 was taken to prolong season length and fishing opportunity. With limited spring quota remaining, inseason action #7 was necessary to ensure that the Chinook salmon quota was not exceeded. Inseason action #4 modified the fishing season consistent with
50 CFR 660.409(b)(1)(i)
.
Inseason Action #8
Description of the action:
Inseason action #8 modified the ocean salmon troll commercial fishery in the area between the United States/Canada border and Cape Falcon.
Effective dates:
Inseason action #8 went into effect on the following dates and remained in effect until stated.
Effective 12:01 a.m., June 19, 2026, through 11:59 p.m., June 23, 2026, the overall NOF landing and possession limit was modified from 35 Chinook salmon per vessel for the open period to 20 Chinook salmon per vessel for the open period.
Effective 11:59 p.m., June 23, 2026, through 11:59 p.m., June 26, 2026, the area between the United States/Canada border and Cape Falcon was closed.
Description of the action:
As of June 16, 2026, the Chinook salmon catch was 35,867 on a spring season quota of 37,300 with 1,433 quota remaining. After assessing available quota and projected effort and catch rates, the fishery was reopened to give vessels an opportunity to access the remaining spring quota. The landing and possession limit was reduced to 20 Chinook salmon per vessel per landing week from 35 Chinook per vessel per landing week. Due to a drop of effort during the previous week and anticipated similar effort for the proposed opening, the fishery reopened for the week of June 19, 2026, through June 23, 2026, without exceeding the spring quota. To avoid exceeding the quota and evaluate the week's landings,
(
printed page 66658)
the fishery in all areas North of Cape Falcon closed on June 23, 2026.
The RA considered the quotas for Chinook salmon stocks, the timing of the action relative to the length of the season, catch and effort to date, projected catch and effort under the proposed action, and other relevant factors like weather, and determined that the inseason action described above was necessary to meet management and conservation goals set preseason. This inseason action modified the number of species that may be caught and landed during specific seasons and the establishment or modification of limited retention regulations under
50 CFR 660.409(b)(1)(ii)
.
With a limited spring quota remaining, inseason action #8 was necessary to ensure that the Chinook salmon quota was not exceeded. Inseason action #4 modified the fishing season consistent with
50 CFR 660.409(b)(1)(i)
.
Inseason Action #9
Description of the action:
Inseason action #9 modified the commercial salmon troll fishery in the area between the United States/Canada border and Cape Falcon, OR.
Effective dates:
Inseason action #9 went into effect on the following dates and remained in effect until superseded or stated.
Effective 12:01 a.m., July 1, 2026, through 11:59 p.m., July 8, 2026, the overall NOF landing and possession limit was 50 Chinook salmon and 50 marked coho salmon per vessel for a landing week Wednesday to Wednesday (modified from Thursday to Wednesday).
Effective 12:01 a.m., July 9, 2026, the overall NOF landing and possession limit was 50 Chinook salmon and 50 marked coho salmon per landing week (Thursday through Wednesday).
Reason and authorization for the action:
In the 2026 annual management measures, for the July through September summer fishery, there were no set landing and possession limits for Chinook salmon for this area. Given the high effort in the troll fleet and the high catch rates observed for much of the spring season, it was deemed prudent to establish a landing and possession limit for the summer season in order to preserve the Chinook quota for the length of the season. NMFS considered the high effort and catch rates seen during the spring season when approving the proposed action of a 50 Chinook salmon landing and possession limit for the first week (July 1, 2026, through July 8, 2026). To meet season length objectives and preserve later fishing opportunity, the limit remained the same for the following week (starting July 9, 2026). In addition, due to the summer season opening on a Wednesday rather than a Thursday, the initial landing week (July 1, 2026, through July 8, 2026) was designated as an 8-day account period. Incorporating the single day into the opening week ensured streamlined catch reporting and maintained consistent data integrity for inseason quota tracking. Beginning July 9, 2026 the fishery resumed the regular Thursday through Wednesday landing week.
The RA considered the 2026 abundance forecasts for Chinook salmon stocks, the timing of the action relative to the length of the season, catch and effort to date, projected catch and effort under the proposed action, and other relevant factors like weather, and determined that these inseason actions described above were necessary to meet management and conservation goals set preseason. These inseason actions modified species caught and landed during specific seasons and the establishment or modification of limited retention regulations under
50 CFR 660.409(b)(1)(ii)
.
Inseason Actions #10-#11
Description of action #10:
Inseason #10 reopened the spring fishery and modified the landing and possession limit for the commercial salmon troll fishery in the area between the United States/Canada border and Cape Falcon from 35 Chinook salmon per vessel for the open period to 20 Chinook salmon per vessel for the open period.
Effective dates:
Inseason #10 went into effect at 12:01 a.m., June 26, 2026, and remained in effect until 11:59 p.m., June 29, 2026.
Reason and Authorization of the Action—See Below
Inseason Action #11
Description of action #11:
Inseason action #11 modified the commercial salmon troll fishery. The area between the United States/Canada border and Cape Falcon was closed.
Effective dates:
Inseason #11 went into effect at 11:59 p.m., on June 29, 2026, and remained in effect until 11:59 p.m., June 30, 2026.
Reason and Authorization of the Action—See Below
Reason and authorization for the actions:
As of June 23, 2026, the Chinook salmon catch was 36,407 for the entire season to date on a spring season quota of 37,300 with 893 quota remaining. After assessing available quota and projected effort and catch rates after the landing week of June 19, 2026, through June 23, 2026, the fishery was reopened to give vessels an opportunity to access the remaining spring quota. To prevent exceeding the quota, the landing and possession limit remained at 20 Chinook salmon per vessel per landing period with a short open period. Due to a drop in effort due to unfavorable weather conditions and the reduction of the landing and possession limit, NMFS determined that the fishery could reopen for the period of June 26, 2026, through June 29, 2026. To avoid exceeding the quota, the fishery closed on June 29, 2026, and remained closed until the end of the spring season on June 30, 2026.
The RA considered the 2026 abundance forecasts for Chinook salmon stocks, the timing of the action relative to the length of the season, catch and effort to date, projected catch and effort under the proposed action, and other relevant factors like weather, and determined that Inseason #10 was necessary to meet management and conservation goals set preseason. Inseason action #10 modified species caught and landed during specific seasons and the establishment or modification of limited retention regulations under
50 CFR 660.409(b)(1)(ii)
. With a limited spring quota remaining, inseason action #11 was necessary to ensure that the Chinook salmon quota was not exceeded, consistent with
50 CFR 660.409(a)
.
All other restrictions and regulations remained in effect as announced for the 2026-2027 ocean salmon fisheries (
91 FR 29092
, May 19, 2026) except as previously modified by inseason actions.
As provided by the inseason notice procedures at
50 CFR 660.411
, actual notice of the described regulatory actions was given, prior to the time the actions became effective, by telephone hotline numbers 206-526-6667 and 800-662-9825, and by U.S. Coast Guard Notice to Mariners broadcasts on Channel 16 VHF-FM and 2182 kHz.
Classification
NMFS issues these actions pursuant to section 305(d) of the MSA. These actions are authorized by
50 CFR 660.409
, which was issued pursuant to section 304(b) of the MSA, and are exempt from review under
Executive Order 12866
. Pursuant to
5 U.S.C. 553(b)(3)(B)
, there is good cause to waive prior notice and an opportunity for public comment on this action, as notice and comment would be impracticable and contrary to the public interest. Prior notice and opportunity
(
printed page 66659)
for public comment on this action was impracticable because NMFS had insufficient time to provide for prior notice and the opportunity for public comment between the time Chinook and coho salmon abundance, catch, and effort information were developed and fisheries impacts were calculated, and the time the fishery modifications had to be implemented in order to ensure fishing opportunity is consistent with conservation needs and management objectives, and/or fisheries are managed consistent with quotas and conservation objectives. There is a heightened need to respond quickly to inseason information about the salmon fishery because fish migrate quickly through the Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) and the mix of stocks in the EEZ shifts throughout the season, thus the time available between the time new information about the fishery becomes available and the opportunity to act effectively on that information is short. By the time public notice and comment would be completed, the mix of stocks in the fishery would have changed such that inseason action would be ineffective and potentially harmful. Therefore, NMFS determined that waiving the notice and comment period in order to respond to updated information indicating the need for immediate action to provide fishing opportunity consistent with quotas and conservation objectives, or to avoid exceeding quotas, served the public interest. As previously noted, actual notice of the regulatory action was provided to fishers through telephone hotlines and radio notifications. These actions comply with the requirements of the annual management measures for ocean salmon fisheries (
90 FR 20810
, May 16, 2025), the FMP, and regulations implementing the FMP under
50 CFR 660.409
and
660.411
. There is good cause under
5 U.S.C. 553(d)(3)
to waive the 30-day delay in effective date, as a delay in effectiveness of this action would constrain fishing in a manner that is inconsistent with the goals of the FMP and the current management measures.

et seq.

Title:
Trafficking Controls and Fraud Investigations (Card Replacement).
OMB Control Number:
0584-0587.
Summary of Collection:
This information collection supports the request to reinstate an expired information collection for an information collection request (ICR). The Food and Nutrition Act of 2008 (the Act), as amended, specifies national eligibility standards and imposes certain administrative requirements on State agencies in administering the Program. The Food and Nutrition Administration (FNA) is still legally required to collect this data and is thereby continuing to collect in violation of the Paperwork Reduction Act.
Federal regulations at 274.6(b)(6) (Appendix A) require that State agencies monitor EBT card replacement requests and send notices to households when they request four cards within a 12-month period. The State agency may determine a threshold for excessive card replacements, which must not to be less than four replacement cards in a 12-month period. alerting the household that their account is being monitored for potential trafficking, misuse, or fraudulent use of Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) benefits.
Need and Use of the Information:
This statement supports the request to reinstate an expired information collection for an information collection related to collection to monitor excessive replacement EBT cards to reduce SNAP fraud waste and abuse by discouraging SNAP benefit trafficking. FNA is still legally required to collect this data and thereby continuing to collect it in violation of the Paperwork Reduction Act.
Per Federal regulations at
7 CFR 274.6(b)(5)
and
7 CFR 274.6(6)
, State agencies must set a threshold on excessive replacement cards and monitor household requests for replacement cards. Once the threshold has been exceeded, the State agency has two options. They may either provide a notice to the client to alert the household that they are monitoring their account for potential, suspicious activity.
If another replacement card is subsequently requested and trafficking is suspected, the State agency shall refer that case to the State's fraud investigation unit. Or the State agency may instead opt to notify the household in writing that the State agency is withholding the card until contact is made. After the household has contacted the State agency, the replacement card will be issued.

In accordance with the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995, BOEM provides the general public and other Federal agencies with an opportunity to comment on new, proposed, revised, and continuing collections of information. Title of Collection:

30 CFR part 553
, Oil Spill Financial Responsibility for Offshore Facilities.”
Abstract:
Title I of the Oil Pollution Act of 1990 (OPA) (
33 U.S.C. 2701
et seq.
) provides at section 1016 that oil spill financial responsibility (OSFR) for offshore facilities be established and maintained according to methods determined acceptable to the President. Section 1016 of the OPA, as amended, supersedes the offshore facility oil spill financial responsibility provisions of the OCS Lands Act. These authorities and responsibilities are among those delegated to BOEM under which BOEM issues regulations governing oil and gas and sulfur operations in the OCS.
This information collection request addresses the regulations at
30 CFR part 553
, Oil Spill Financial Responsibility for Offshore Facilities. BOEM collects the information to ensure proper and efficient administration of its oil spill financial responsibility requirements. BOEM collects this information to:
Provide a standard method for establishing whether a party is required to demonstrate oil spill financial responsibility for offshore facilities;
Identify and maintain a record of those offshore facilities that have a potential oil spill liability requiring the demonstration of oil spill financial responsibility;
Establish and maintain a continuous record of evidence of oil spill financial responsibility to assure payment of claims for oil spill cleanup and damages resulting from operations conducted on covered offshore facilities and from the transportation of oil from covered offshore facilities;
Establish and maintain a continuous record of responsible parties, as defined in Title I of the Oil Pollution Act of 1990, and their agents or authorized representatives for oil spill financial responsibility for covered offshore facilities; and
Establish and maintain a continuous record of persons to contact and U.S. agents for service of process for claims associated with oil spills from covered offshore facilities.
BOEM uses the information collected under
30 CFR part 553
to verify compliance with section 1016 of OPA. This information is necessary to confirm that designated applicants can cover cleanup costs and damages resulting from hydrocarbon discharges originating from offshore facilities. BOEM uses these forms to ensure the effective and efficient administration of oil spill financial responsibility requirements.
BOEM is revising Forms BOEM-1019 (Insurance Certificate), BOEM-1020 (Surety Bond), and BOEM-1023 (Financial Guarantee) to reflect updated requirements for oil spill financial responsibility, expressly tying the applicable coverage period to when an incident begins. The revisions align the forms with BOEM's updated policy that OSFR coverage going forward will be applicable only in relation to each incident first occurring on or after the effective date of the applicable OSFR instrument and on or before its termination. These changes do not apply retroactively to OSFR providers on earlier iterations of the forms.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Codification of Nevada's Approved Underground Storage Tank Program
A. What is codification?
Codification is the process of placing citations and references to a State's statutes and regulations that comprise a State's approved UST program into the Code of Federal Regulations (CFR). The EPA codifies its approval of State programs in
40 CFR part 282
and incorporates by reference State statutes and regulations that the EPA can enforce, after the approval is final, under sections 9005 and 9006 of RCRA, and any other applicable statutory provisions. The incorporation by reference of EPA-approved State programs in the CFR should substantially enhance the public's ability to discern the status of the approved State UST programs and State requirements that can be federally enforced. This effort provides clear notice to the public of the scope of the approved program in each State.
B. What is the history of codification of Nevada's UST Program?
The EPA originally approved the Nevada UST Program on December 24, 1992 (
57 FR 61376
). This approval was effective on March 30, 1993. The EPA then incorporated by reference and codified Nevada's approved UST program on July 17, 1998 (
63 FR 38500
), effective September 15, 1998. Nevada revised its UST program in response to revisions to the Federal UST regulations published in a final rule on July 15, 2015 (
80 FR 41566
). On November 20, 2018, in accordance with
40 CFR 281.51(a)
, Nevada submitted an application seeking the EPA's approval for its revised UST Program. On July 29, 2021, Nevada submitted amendments to the application, based on comments from the EPA. On September 30, 2021, the EPA granted final approval to Nevada's revised UST Program (
86 FR 54107
), effective November 29, 2021. Through this action, the EPA is amending
40 CFR 282.78
to incorporate by reference and codify Nevada's revised UST Program.
C. What codification decisions is the EPA making in this rule?
In this rule, the EPA is finalizing regulatory text that incorporates by reference Nevada's revised and federally approved UST Program. In accordance with the requirements of
1 CFR 51.5
, the EPA is incorporating by reference Nevada's regulations as described in the
(
printed page 66653)
amendments to
40 CFR part 282
set forth below.
Specifically, in
40 CFR 282.78(d)(1)(i)
, the EPA is incorporating by reference portions of Nevada Administrative Code, Chapter 445A—Water Controls and Nevada Administrative Code, Chapter 459—Hazardous Materials. These regulations, which are part of Nevada's approved UST Program, establish the rules that Nevada uses to regulate underground storage tanks and in particular, to prevent and respond to releases from such tanks. The text of the regulations that EPA is incorporating by reference can be found in the document titled, “Nevada Regulatory Requirements Applicable to the Underground Storage Tank Program,” dated July 29, 2021. This document is available through
https://www.regulations.gov
by searching on EPA-R09-UST-2025-0703 and by contacting the individual listed in the
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT
provision of this preamble. Section 282.78(d)(1)(ii) of 40 CFR identifies the Nevada statutes and regulations that are part of the approved UST Program, although not incorporated by reference for enforcement purposes. Section 282.78(d)(1)(iii) of 40 CFR identifies the Nevada statutory and regulatory provisions that are broader in scope and therefore not incorporated by reference.
Sections 282.78(d)(2) through (5) of 40 CFR reference the Attorney General's Statement, Demonstration of Adequate Enforcement Procedures, Program Description, and Memorandum of Agreement, which are part of Nevada's Application and part of the Nevada UST Program under subtitle I of RCRA. These materials are available through
https://www.regulations.gov
by searching on EPA-R09-UST-2021-0597, or by contacting the individual listed in the
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT
provision of this preamble.
D. What is the effect of the EPA's codification of the federally approved Nevada UST Program on enforcement?
The EPA retains the authority under sections 9003(h), 9005, and 9006 of subtitle I of RCRA,
42 U.S.C. 6991b(h)
,
6991d
, and
6991e
, and other applicable statutory and regulatory provisions, to undertake corrective action, inspections, and enforcement actions, and to issue orders in approved States. If the EPA determines it will take such actions in Nevada, the EPA will rely on Federal sanctions, Federal inspection authorities, and other Federal procedures rather than the State analogs. Therefore, the EPA is not incorporating by reference Nevada's procedural and enforcement authorities, although they are listed in
40 CFR 282.78(d)(1)(ii)
.
E. What is a “broader in scope” provision?
States may enact laws that are more stringent than their Federal counterparts (
See
RCRA section 9008,
42 U.S.C. 6991g
). When an approved State program includes requirements that are considered more stringent than those required by Federal law, the more stringent requirements become part of the federally approved program in accordance with
40 CFR 281.12(a)(3)(i)
.
In addition, States may enact laws which are broader in scope than their Federal counterparts in accordance with
40 CFR 281.12(a)(3)(ii)
. State requirements that go beyond the scope of the Federal program are broader in scope. These requirements are not part of the federally approved program, and the EPA cannot enforce them. Although broader in scope requirements in Nevada's UST Program are enforceable by Nevada in accordance with Nevada law, they are not Federal RCRA requirements.
F. What State provisions are not part of the codification?
As discussed above in sections I.C. and I.E. of this preamble, some provisions of Nevada's UST Program are not part of the federally approved UST Program because they are broader in scope than the Federal UST Program. Where an approved State program has provisions that are broader in scope than the Federal program, those provisions are not a part of the federally approved program. As a result, State provisions which are broader in scope than the Federal program are not incorporated by reference in
40 CFR part 282
for purposes of enforcement (
See
40 CFR 281.12(a)(3)(ii)
). For reference and clarity,
40 CFR 282.78(d)(1)(iii)
lists the Nevada statutory and regulatory provisions which are broader in scope than the Federal program. These provisions are, therefore, not part of the approved UST Program that the EPA is codifying. Although these provisions cannot be enforced by the EPA, Nevada will continue to implement and enforce such provisions under Nevada law.
II. Statutory and Executive Order (E.O.) Reviews
The EPA's action merely codifies Nevada's revised UST Program requirements pursuant to RCRA section 9004, and it does not impose additional requirements other than those imposed by Nevada law. For that reason, this action:

In addition, this action does not apply on any Indian reservation land or in any other area where the EPA or an Indian Tribe has demonstrated that a Tribe has jurisdiction. In those areas of Indian country, the final rule does not have Tribal implications and will not impose substantial direct costs on Tribal governments or preempt Tribal law as specified by

AGENCY:
Environmental Protection Agency (EPA).
ACTION:
Notice of tentative approval and solicitation of requests for a public hearing.
SUMMARY:
Notice is hereby given that the State of Arkansas is revising its approved Public Water System Supervision (PWSS) program. Arkansas has adopted the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) drinking water rules for the Consumer Confidence Report Rule Revisions. Therefore, the EPA intends to approve this PWSS program revision package.
DATES:
Comments or a request for a public hearing must be submitted by November 23, 2026 to the Regional Administrator at the EPA Region 6 address shown below.
ADDRESSES:
All documents relating to this determination are available for inspection between the hours of 8 a.m. and 4:30 p.m., Monday through Friday, at the following offices: Arkansas Department of Health, Engineering Branch, 4815 W Markham, Little Rock, Arkansas 72205; and United States Environmental Protection Agency, Region 6, Drinking Water Section (6WD-DD), 1201 Elm Street, Suite 500, Dallas, Texas 75270.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Jatin H. Mistry, EPA Region 6, Drinking Water Section at the Dallas address given above; by telephone at (214) 665-7483; or by email at
mistry.jatin@epa.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Frivolous or insubstantial requests for a hearing may be denied by the Regional Administrator. However, if a substantial request for a public hearing is made by November 23, 2026, a public hearing will be held. If no timely and appropriate request for a hearing is received and the Regional Administrator does not elect to hold a hearing on his own motion, this determination shall become final and effective. EPA will publish a document in the
Federal Register
announcing the date this determination becomes final and effective.
Any request for a public hearing shall include the following information: (1) The name, address, and telephone number of the individual, organization, or other entity requesting a hearing; (2) a brief statement of the requesting person's interest in the Regional Administrator's determination, and a brief statement of the information that the requesting person intends to submit at such hearing; and (3) the signature of the individual making the request, or, if the request is made on behalf of an organization or other entity, the signature of a responsible official of the organization or other entity.
Arkansas has adopted the EPA drinking water rules for the Consumer Confidence Report Rule Revisions. The
(
printed page 66698)
EPA has determined that the Consumer Confidence Report Rule Revisions submitted by Arkansas are no less stringent than the corresponding Federal regulations. Therefore, the EPA intends to approve this PWSS program revision package.

AGENCY:
U.S. Customs and Border Protection, Department of Homeland Security.
ACTION:
Final rule; extension of compliance date.
SUMMARY:
This document announces that U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) will extend the compliance date for the regulatory provisions mandating the formal entry of merchandise arriving through the international postal network that is subject to partner government agency requirements, subject to duties under Chapter 98 or Chapter 99 of the
(
printed page 66639)
Harmonized Tariff Schedule of the United States (HTSUS), or for which duty-free treatment is claimed under Chapter 98 of the HTSUS or pursuant to a Free Trade Agreement, which were published in the
Federal Register
on June 24, 2026. We believe the public will benefit from more time to prepare for compliance with these changes.
DATES:
The compliance date for
19 CFR 145.12(a)(2)(v)
and
(vi)
is January 20, 2027.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Christopher Mabelitini, Intellectual Property Rights & E-Commerce Division, Office of Trade, U.S. Customs and Border Protection, 202-325-6915,
ecommerce@cbp.dhs.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Background
On June 24, 2026, U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) published an interim final rule in the
Federal Register
(
91 FR 37801
) implementing in CBP regulations an indefinite suspension of the
de minimis
administrative exemption under
19 U.S.C. 1321(a)(2)(C)
for merchandise arriving through the international postal network.
[
1
]
Further, to accommodate the entry of merchandise formerly eligible for the
de minimis
administrative exemption, the interim final rule established a new informal entry process for merchandise valued at $2,500 or less entering the United States through the mail environment, including shipments that would previously have been eligible for the
de minimis
exemption.
[
2
]
The suspension of the
de minimis
administrative exemption took effect on June 24, 2026. The remainder of the interim final rule was effective on July 24, 2026.
In the interim final rule, CBP made certain shipments ineligible for the new informal entry process for postal shipments. Merchandise subject to Partner Government Agency (PGA) requirements, merchandise subject to duties under Chapter 98 or Chapter 99 of the Harmonized Tariff Schedule of the United States (HTSUS), or for which duty-free treatment is claimed under Chapter 98 of the HTSUS or pursuant to a Free Trade Agreement, are ineligible for the postal informal entry procedures adopted in the interim final rule.
[
3
]
However, in recognition of the time needed for the public to adjust to this formal entry requirement, CBP delayed the compliance date for
19 CFR 145.12(a)(2)(v)
and
(vi)
to October 22, 2026. In consideration of the business process changes necessary to achieve full compliance, CBP provided for a delayed compliance date to allow time for the trade to adjust to the new requirement.
CBP has determined that a further extension of this compliance date is needed to give importers, brokers, and logistics providers in the international postal network additional time to update their internal systems, develop policies and procedures for submission of relevant data, and to develop the technological infrastructure needed to comply with these requirements. Failure to afford the public extra time to comply with these requirements could lead to disruptions in the flow of important international postal shipments destined to Americans. For this reason, CBP is extending the date for compliance with
19 CFR 145.12(a)(2)(v)
and
(vi)
to January 20, 2027.
II. Administrative Procedure Act
The Administrative Procedure Act (APA),
5 U.S.C. 551
et seq.,
generally requires agencies to publish a notice of proposed rulemaking in the
Federal Register
and provide interested persons the opportunity to submit comments prior to issuing a final rule. The APA provides an exception to advance notice and comment requirements “when the agency for good cause finds (and incorporates the finding and a brief statement of reasons therefor in the rules issued) that notice and public comment thereon are impracticable, unnecessary, or contrary to the public interest.”
5 U.S.C. 553(b)(B)
. CBP finds that good cause exists to issue this document as a final rule under the APA's good cause exception, because notice and comment are impracticable.
Providing notice and a public comment period on whether the compliance date should be delayed is impracticable because the current compliance date would have passed within the time needed to permit the solicitation of public comments on this rule. Because the public comment period would overtake the current compliance deadline of October 22, 2026, importers, brokers, and logistics providers in the international postal network would still be required to come into compliance with
19 CFR 145.12(a)(2)(v)
and
(vi)
by October 22, 2026. Those importers and other parties who need additional time to comply would not be able to benefit from the extended compliance period that this rule provides.
Additionally, this rule does not impose any new substantive regulatory requirements on any person and merely reflects the extension of the compliance date for
19 CFR 145.12(a)(2)(v)
and
(vi)
as set forth in the interim final rule published on June 24, 2026 (
91 FR 37801
). An extension of this compliance date is needed to give importers and other parties additional time to update internal systems, revise business practices, and develop technological infrastructure needed to comply with CBP's requirements. Providing immediate certainty that this compliance date is extended is therefore needed to ensure that importers and other parties avoid incurring unnecessary costs, burdens, and other challenges associated with meeting the initial compliance date. The delayed compliance date does not change the process that importers and other parties currently use for informal mail entries, as established by the interim final rule
(
printed page 66640)
published on June 24, 2026 (
91 FR 37801
), during this period of delay.
The delayed compliance date also does not impose a burden on importers or other parties who have already come into compliance or had planned to come into compliance by October 22, 2026. Importers or other parties may voluntarily come into compliance at an earlier date if they have the processes already in place. Importers or other parties who do not have processes already in place will have until January 20, 2027, to comply with the requirements found in § 145.12(a)(2)(v) and (vi). Accordingly, importers and other parties who have not yet established the necessary processes will have additional time to comply with the requirements of § 145.12(a)(2)(v) and (vi), which provides further flexibility to the trade community as it transitions to these new requirements.
CBP also finds that the delayed compliance date does not conflict with the serious public health and safety implications that CBP outlined in the interim final rule published on June 24, 2026 (
91 FR 37801
). Because the informal entry process established by the interim final rule will remain in place during this period of delay, the dangers that justified the suspension of
de minimis
exception for mail remain addressed.
Thus, this rule is exempt from the prior public notice and comment requirements of the APA under the good cause exception.
5 U.S.C. 553(b)(B)
.
III. Signing Authority
In accordance with Treasury Order 100-20, the Secretary of the Treasury delegated to the Secretary of Homeland Security the authority related to the customs revenue functions vested in the Secretary of the Treasury as set forth in
6 U.S.C. 212
and
215
, subject to certain exceptions. This regulation is being issued in accordance with DHS Delegation 07010.3, Revision 03.2, which delegates to the Commissioner of CBP the authority to prescribe and approve regulations related to customs revenue functions.
Rodney S. Scott, Commissioner, having reviewed and approved this document, has delegated the authority to electronically sign this document to Susan S. Thomas, Executive Assistant Commissioner, Office of Trade, for purposes of publication in the
Federal Register
.
Susan S. Thomas,
Executive Assistant Commissioner, Office of Trade, U.S. Customs and Border Protection.

(Aug. 5, 2025)), as modified by
E.O. 14388
of February 20, 2026 (Continuing the Suspension of Duty-Free De Minimis Treatment for All Countries,

                         Informal entry procedures are authorized by
19 U.S.C. 1498(a)(1)(A)
for shipments of merchandise valued at $2,500 or less, and may incorporate formal entry procedures appearing in
19 U.S.C. 1484
and
1485
. The Secretary of the Treasury is authorized to “prescribe rules and regulations for the declaration and entry of merchandise when the aggregate value of the shipment does not exceed an amount specified . . . by regulation, but not more than $2,500.” See
19 U.S.C. 1498(a)(1)(A)
. The Homeland Security Act of 2002 (HSA) generally transferred the functions of the U.S. Customs Service from the Treasury Department to the Secretary of Homeland Security. See
Public Law 107-296
, 116 Stat. 2142;
6 U.S.C. 203
(“there shall be transferred to the Secretary [of Homeland Security] the functions . . . of (1) the United States Customs Service of the Department of the Treasury, including the functions of the Secretary of the Treasury relating thereto”). Nevertheless, pursuant to Section 412 of the HSA, the Treasury Department retained authority related to various customs revenue functions, including those functions found in the Tariff Act of 1930, Public Law 71-361, 46 Stat. 590, as amended (codified at
19 U.S.C. 1202
et seq.
).
6 U.S.C. 212(a)(1)
, (2). But the Secretary of the Treasury may delegate any such retained authority at the Secretary's discretion.
6 U.S.C. 212(a)(1)
. Consistent with this delegation authority, the Secretary of the Treasury issued Treasury Order 100-20 (available at
https://home.treasury.gov/​about/​general-information/​orders-and-directives/​treasury-order-100-20
), delegating the authorities contained in
6 U.S.C. 212
and
215
to the Secretary of Homeland Security.
Back to Citation
3.
    
                         Concurrently with the interim final rule, CBP announced a test of a new voluntary electronic mail process for qualified shipments valued at $2,500 or less, known as the Entry Type 13 test.
91 FR 38007
(Jun. 24, 2026). For eligible types of shipments, this test provides an optional alternative to filing formal entry. The Entry Type 13 test began on September 22, 2026. Accordingly, at the end of the delayed compliance window, filers may choose to file formal entry (in accordance with
19 CFR 145.12(a)(2)(v)
and
(vi)
) or participate in the Entry Type 13 test for eligible shipments.
