Securities and Exchange Commission
[Release No. 34-106691; File No. SR-NYSE-2026-51]
October 19, 2026.
Pursuant to Section 19(b)(1)
[
1
]
of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (“Act”)
[
2
]
and Rule 19b-4 thereunder,
[
3
]
notice is hereby given that on October 9, 2026, New York Stock Exchange LLC (“NYSE” or the “Exchange”) filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission (the “Commission”) the proposed rule change as described in Items I, II, and III below, which Items have been prepared by the Exchange. The Commission is publishing this notice to solicit comments on the proposed rule change from interested persons.
(
printed page 66749)
I. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Terms of Substance of the Proposed Rule Change
The Exchange proposes to harmonize NYSE Rule 3220 (Influencing or Rewarding Employees of Others) with certain changes by the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority, Inc. (“FINRA”) to FINRA Rule 3220 to, among other things, increase the gift limit from $100 to $300. The proposed rule change is available on the Exchange's website at
www.nyse.com
and at the principal office of the Exchange.
II. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
In its filing with the Commission, the self-regulatory organization included statements concerning the purpose of, and basis for, the proposed rule change and discussed any comments it received on the proposed rule change. The text of those statements may be examined at the places specified in Item IV below. The Exchange has prepared summaries, set forth in sections A, B, and C below, of the most significant parts of such statements.
A. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and the Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
1. Purpose
This proposed rule change is based on a filing recently submitted by FINRA, and approved by the Commission, to amend FINRA Rule 3220 (Influencing or Rewarding Employees of Others), and is intended to harmonize the Exchange's rules with those of FINRA so as to promote uniform standards across the securities industry.
[
4
]
The Exchange proposes to harmonize NYSE Rule 3220 (Influencing or Rewarding Employees of Others) with certain changes by FINRA to FINRA Rule 3220 to increase the gift limit from $100 to $300. Additionally, unlike FINRA Rule 3220, current NYSE Rule 3220 does not include provisions covering: supervision and recordkeeping; gifts incidental to business entertainment; valuation of gifts; aggregation of gifts; personal gifts; bereavement gifts;
de minimis
gifts and promotional or commemorative items; donations due to federally declared major disasters; or gifts to a member or member organization's associated persons or individual retail customers. To further harmonize its rules with FINRA, the Exchange proposes to adopt these provisions in proposed Supplementary Material .01 through .09 to NYSE Rule 3220 that is substantially similar to Supplementary Material .01 through .09 to FINRA Rule 3220 adopted in the FINRA Rule Change.
Pursuant to Rule 17d-2 under the Act,
[
5
]
the Exchange and FINRA have entered into an agreement to allocate regulatory responsibility for common rules (the “17d-2 Agreement”). The 17d-2 Agreement covers common members
[
6
]
of the Exchange and FINRA and allocates to FINRA regulatory responsibility, with respect to common members, for the following: (i) examination of common members of the Exchange and FINRA for compliance with certain federal securities laws, rules and regulations and rules of the Exchange that the Exchange has certified as identical or substantially similar to FINRA rules; (ii) investigation of common members of the Exchange and FINRA for violations of certain federal securities laws, rules or regulations, or Exchange rules that the Exchange has certified as identical or substantially similar to a FINRA rule; and (iii) enforcement of compliance by common members with certain federal securities laws, rules and regulations, and the rules of the Exchange that the Exchange has certified as identical or substantially similar to FINRA rules.
[
7
]
NYSE Rule 3220 is based on FINRA Rule 3220.
[
8
]
NYSE Rule 3220(a) states that no member, member organization, or person associated with a member organization, shall, directly or indirectly, give or permit to be given anything of value, including gratuities, in excess of one hundred dollars per individual per year to any person, principal, proprietor, employee, agent to representative of another person where such payment or gratuity is in relation to the business of the employer of the recipient of the payment or gratuity. NYSE Rule 3220(b) provides for certain exceptions from the requirements enumerated in Rule 3220(a). Finally, NYSE Rule 3220(c) requires a member or member organization to maintain a record of payments or gratuities of any amount for a specified period of time.
The Exchange believes that harmonizing NYSE Rule 3220 with FINRA Rule 3220 will help to avoid confusion among Exchange members and member organizations that are also members of FINRA. The proposed changes to NYSE Rule 3220 are also designed to enable the Exchange to incorporate the entirety of NYSE Rule 3220 in the 17d-2 Agreement, further reducing duplicative regulation of members and member organizations that are also members of FINRA. For the avoidance of doubt, NYSE Rule 3220 would equally apply to Exchange-only members and member organizations as the Exchange believes it appropriately protects against improprieties, such as conflicts of interest, that might arise when a member or member organization or person associated with a member organization gives items of value to an employee of another person, such as an institutional customer, vendor or counterparty with the hope of strengthening the relationship with the customer.
As amended, like FINRA Rule 3220(a), paragraph (a) of NYSE Rule 3220 would prohibit gifts in excess of $300 per individual per year where the gift or gratuity is in relation to the business of the employer of the recipient.
Additionally, the Exchange proposes to adopt Supplementary Material .01 through .09 to NYSE Rule 3220 to codify the provisions within FINRA Supplementary Materials 3220.01 through 3220.09. More specifically, proposed Supplementary Material .01 through .09 to NYSE Rule 3220, like FINRA Supplementary Materials 3220.01 through 3220.09, would codify the FINRA Supplementary Materials to Rule 3220 related to gifts incidental to business entertainment, valuation of gifts, aggregation of gifts, personal gifts, bereavement gifts,
de minimis
gifts and promotional or commemorative items, donations due to federally declared major disasters, supervision and recordkeeping, and gifts to a Member's or Member Organization's associated persons or individual retail customers.
Proposed Supplementary Material .01 (Gifts Incidental to Business Entertainment) would state that a gift given during the course of a business entertainment event is subject to Rule 3220 unless it is consistent with the
(
printed page 66750)
requirements of proposed Supplementary Material .04 (Personal Gifts) or .06 (
De Minimis
Gifts and Promotional or Commemorative Items) which is substantially similar to FINRA Rule 3220 Supplementary Material .04 and .06. For the purpose of the $300 limit, the cost of the business entertainment event itself would not be included in the value of the gift.
Proposed Supplementary Material .02 (Valuation of Gifts) would require members and member organizations to value gifts (other than tickets for sporting or other events) at cost, exclusive of tax and delivery charges, and would require members and member organizations to value tickets for sporting or other events at the higher of cost or face value. If gifts are given to multiple recipients, members and member organizations must record the names of each recipient and calculate and record the value of the gift on a pro-rata, per-recipient basis, for purposes of ensuring compliance with the $300 limit in Rule 3220(a). FINRA Rule 3220 at Supplementary Material .02 requires Members to value gifts (other than tickets for sporting or other events) at cost rather than at the higher of cost or market value reduces complexity and subjectivity because market value can be difficult and burdensome to determine, while distinguishing tickets for sporting or other events accounts for the fact that such tickets are commonly purchased on secondary markets at costs that differ from face value.
Proposed Supplementary Material .03 (Aggregation of Gifts) would require members and member organizations to aggregate all gifts given by the member, member organization and each person associated with a member organization to a particular recipient over the course of the year for purposes of ensuring compliance with the $300 limit in Rule 3220(a), and would require each member and member organization to state in its procedures whether it is aggregating all gifts given by the member, member organization and each person associated with a member organization on a calendar year, fiscal year, or on a rolling basis beginning with the first gift to any particular recipient. The aggregation requirement would not apply to personal gifts under proposed Supplementary Material .04 or to gifts of
de minimis
value or promotional or commemorative items under proposed Supplementary Material .06 as they are already not subject to the gift limit. This proposed provision, which is substantially similar to FINRA Rule 3220(a), would help ensure that persons who give multiple gifts in a year to the same recipient do not circumvent the gift limit.
Proposed Supplementary Material .04 (Personal Gifts) would state that gifts that are given for infrequent life events (
e.g.,
a wedding gift or a congratulatory gift for the birth of a child) are not subject to the restrictions in Rule 3220(a) or the recordkeeping requirements in Rule 3220(c), provided the gifts are customary and reasonable, personal in nature, and not in relation to the business of the employer of the recipient. In determining whether a gift is “personal in nature and not in relation to the business of the employer of the recipient,” members or member organization should consider a number of factors, including the nature of any pre-existing personal or family relationship between the person giving the gift and the recipient and whether the associated person paid for the gift. When the member or member organization bears the cost of the gift, either directly or by reimbursing an associated person, the Exchange will presume that such gift is not personal in nature and instead is in relation to the business of the employer of the recipient. This provision is substantially similar to FINRA Rule 3220 at Supplementary Material .04.
Proposed Supplementary Material .05 (Bereavement Gifts) separates bereavement gifts from personal gifts. Proposed Supplementary Material .05 would state that bereavement gifts that are customary and reasonable are not considered to be in relation to the business of the employer of the recipient and, therefore, are not subject to the restrictions in Rule 3220(a) or the recordkeeping requirements in Rule 3220(c). This provision is substantially similar to FINRA Rule 3220 at Supplementary Material .05.
Proposed Supplementary Material .06 (
De Minimis
Gifts and Promotional or Commemorative Items), at paragraph (a), would state that gifts of a
de minimis
value (
e.g.,
pens, notepads, or modest desk ornaments) or promotional items of nominal value that display the member's or member organization's logo (
e.g.,
umbrellas, tote bags, or shirts) are not subject to the restrictions in Rule 3220(a) or the recordkeeping requirements in Rule 3220(c), provided that the value of the gift or promotional item is substantially below the $300 limit. Proposed Supplementary Material .06(b) would state that customary and reasonable solely decorative items commemorating a business transaction are not subject to the restrictions in Rule 3220(a) or the recordkeeping requirements in Rule 3220(c). These provisions are substantially similar to FINRA Rule 3220 at Supplementary Material .06.
Proposed Supplementary Material .07 (Donations Due to Federally Declared Major Disasters) would state that donations by a member, member organization, or person associated with a member organization to any person, principal, proprietor, employee, agent or representative of another person to provide assistance to the individual for losses sustained in a natural event that the President has declared to be a major disaster, such as a wildfire, hurricane, tornado, earthquake, or flood, are not considered “in relation to the business of the employer of the recipient” for purposes of Rule 3220(a) and are not subject to the restrictions in Rule 3220(a) or the recordkeeping requirements of Rule 3220(c). This provision is substantially similar to FINRA Rule 3220 at Supplementary Material .07 which recognizes that the nature of such disasters is unpredictable and catastrophic.
Proposed Supplementary Material .08 (Supervision and Recordkeeping) would state that Rule 3110 requires member organizations to have a supervisory system reasonably designed to achieve compliance with applicable securities laws and regulations and Exchange rules, including Rule 3220. To meet these standards, member organizations would be required to have systems and procedures reasonably designed to ensure that payments and gratuities in relation to the business of the employer of the recipient given by the member organization or persons associated with a member organization to employees of another person are (a) reported to the member organization; (b) reviewed for compliance with Rule 3220; and (c) maintained in the member organization's records. Such procedures must be reasonably designed to ensure that an associated person who is giving a payment or gratuity is not responsible for determining whether such payment or gratuity is in relation to the business of the recipient's employer. Member organizations are not required to maintain records of gifts that are consistent with the requirements of proposed Supplementary Material .04 through .07 of Rule 3220. Requiring a person other than the associated person giving the gift to assess the nature of the gift is intended to encourage objectivity in making such determinations, consistent with existing FINRA guidance.
Proposed Supplementary Material .09 (Gifts to a Member Organization's Associated Persons or Individual Retail Customers) would state that Rule 3220 does not apply to gifts from a member
(
printed page 66751)
organization to its own associated persons, or to gifts from a member organization or person associated with a member organization to individual retail customers. The Exchange believes that proposed Supplementary Material .09 would clarify, and improve awareness and understanding of, the scope of Rule 3220, consistent with FINRA Rule 3220 at Supplementary Material .09.
The Exchange notes that, although the FINRA Rule Change provides authority for FINRA to grant exemptive relief to FINRA Rule 3220, the Exchange's proposed rule change would not harmonize or align with FINRA through the inclusion of a corresponding provision.
[
9
]
The Exchange notes that, historically, it has not always aligned with FINRA with respect to providing exemptive relief to member organizations and in fact, has provided exemptive relief in very limited circumstances to member organizations, as illustrated in NYSE Rule 9610.
The Exchange believes the proposed rule change would promote efficiency without reducing protection for investors and the public interest. The proposed changes to NYSE Rule 3220 to conform to the rules of FINRA improve transparency, awareness, and understanding of NYSE Rule 3220's requirements. The Exchange believes these proposed changes would also help facilitate compliance with NYSE Rule 3220 and would provide regulatory certainty to members and member organizations.
2. Statutory Basis
The proposed rule change is consistent with Section 6(b) of the Act,
[
10
]
in general, and furthers the objectives of Section 6(b)(5),
[
11
]
in particular, because it is designed to prevent fraudulent and manipulative acts and practices, to promote just and equitable principles of trade, to foster cooperation and coordination with persons engaged in facilitating transactions in securities, to remove impediments to, and perfect the mechanism of, a free and open market and a national market system and, in general, to protect investors and the public interest.
The Exchange believes that the proposed rule change will further these requirements by providing greater harmonization between Exchange and FINRA rules of similar purpose, resulting in greater uniformity and less burdensome and more efficient regulatory compliance. As such, the proposed rule change would foster cooperation and coordination with persons engaged in facilitating transactions in securities and would remove impediments to and perfect the mechanism of a free and open market and a national market system in accordance with Section 6(b)(5) of the Act.
[
12
]
As noted above, the proposed rule change to amend current NYSE Rule 3220 is designed to conform the Exchange's Rule to the comparable FINRA rule. The Exchange also notes the changes proposed herein align NYSE Rule 3220 with a recent filing submitted by FINRA and approved by the Commission.
[
13
]
As described above, the Exchange believes the proposed change to amend current Exchange Rule 3220 to conform to FINRA Rule 3220 is consistent with the Act because it is intended to harmonize the Exchange Rule with the comparable FINRA rule and will promote uniform standards across the securities industry. The Exchange also believes the proposed change to adopt Supplementary Material .01 through .09 to Exchange Rule 3220 is consistent with the Act because it is a conforming change to adopt the provisions within FINRA Supplementary Materials 3220.01 through 3220.09. The Exchange further believes that these changes will help to reduce and avoid potential confusion among members, member organizations, and persons associated with member organizations of the Exchange that are also members of FINRA by harmonizing Exchange Rule 3220 with FINRA Rule 3220. The proposed rule change is designed to enable the Exchange to incorporate Exchange Rule 3220 into the 17d-2 Agreement, further reducing duplicative regulation of members, member organizations, and persons associated with member organizations that are also members of FINRA. For the avoidance of doubt, Exchange Rule 3220 would equally apply to Exchange-only members and member organizations as the Exchange believes it appropriately protects against improprieties that might arise when substantial gifts or monetary payments are given to certain persons.
The Exchange believes the proposed rule change would promote efficiency without reducing protection for investors and the public interest. The proposed changes to Exchange Rule 3220 to conform to the rules of FINRA improve transparency, awareness, and understanding of the Exchange Rule's requirements. The Exchange believes these proposed changes would also help facilitate compliance with NYSE Rule 3220.
B. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Burden on Competition
The Exchange does not believe that the proposed rule change will impose any burden on competition that is not necessary or appropriate in furtherance of the purposes of the Act. The proposed rule change is not designed to address any competitive issues but rather to provide greater harmonization among Exchange and FINRA rules of similar purpose, resulting in less burdensome and more efficient regulatory compliance for common members and facilitating FINRA's performance of its regulatory functions under the 17d-2 Agreement. As such, the Exchange does not believe that the proposed rule change will impose any burden on competition not necessary or appropriate in furtherance of the purposes of the Act.
C. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Comments on the Proposed Rule Change Received From Members, Participants, or Others
No written comments were solicited or received with respect to the proposed rule change.
III. Date of Effectiveness of the Proposed Rule Change and Timing for Commission Action
The Exchange has filed the proposed rule change pursuant to Section 19(b)(3)(A)(iii) of the Act
[
14
]
and Rule 19b-4(f)(6) thereunder.
[
15
]
Because the proposed rule change does not: (i) significantly affect the protection of investors or the public interest; (ii) impose any significant burden on competition; and (iii) become operative prior to 30 days from the date on which it was filed, or such shorter time as the Commission may designate, if consistent with the protection of investors and the public interest, the proposed rule change has become effective pursuant to Section 19(b)(3)(A) of the Act and Rule 19b-4(f)(6)(iii) thereunder.
(
printed page 66752)
A proposed rule change filed under Rule 19b-4(f)(6)
[
16
]
normally does not become operative prior to 30 days after the date of the filing. However, pursuant to Rule 19b-4(f)(6)(iii),
[
17
]
the Commission may designate a shorter time if such action is consistent with the protection of investors and the public interest.
At any time within 60 days of the filing of such proposed rule change, the Commission summarily may temporarily suspend such rule change if it appears to the Commission that such action is necessary or appropriate in the public interest, for the protection of investors, or otherwise in furtherance of the purposes of the Act. If the Commission takes such action, the Commission shall institute proceedings under Section 19(b)(2)(B)
[
18
]
of the Act to determine whether the proposed rule change should be approved or disapproved.

Do not include personal identifiable information in submissions; you should submit only information that you wish to make available publicly. AGENCY:
U.S. Customs and Border Protection, Department of Homeland Security.
ACTION:
General notice.
SUMMARY:
This document announces that U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) is modifying the test of the new electronic informal entry type for merchandise entering the United States through the international mail process to permit transmission of the entry with or without electronic Partner Government Agency (PGA) data.
DATES:
The modification is effective on October 22, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Christopher Mabelitini, Director, Intellectual Property Rights & E-Commerce Division, Office of Trade, U.S. Customs and Border Protection, 202-325-6915,
ecommerce@cbp.dhs.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
On June 24, 2026, U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) published a notice in the
Federal Register
(
91 FR 38007
), announcing a test for a new electronic informal entry process for international mail in the Automated Commercial Environment (ACE), the entry type 13 (Informal Mail Entry). The test commenced on September 22, 2026. The new informal entry type 13 is available for international mail shipments valued at $2,500 or less, including those shipments that would previously have been eligible for the
de minimis
duty exemption, that are sent to the United States through the international postal network (“international mail”). The Entry Type 13 Test provides an alternative to the interim process for informal mail entries, as set forth in section 145.12(b) of
title 19 of the Code of Federal Regulations
(
19 CFR 145.12(b)
), and allows filers to file informal entry for qualified international mail shipments electronically in ACE. This test temporarily creates an informal entry pathway for low-value international mail shipments subject to PGA data requirements or duties other than those set forth in Chapters 1-97 of the Harmonized Tariff Schedule of the United States (HTSUS),
[
1
]
which are ineligible for the interim process for informal mail entries, pursuant to
19 CFR 145.12(a)(2)(v)-(vi)
.
To participate in the test, the importer of record (IOR), who is the owner, purchaser of the merchandise being mailed to the United States, or the licensed broker properly appointed by the owner, purchaser, or consignee, who is acting as an IOR, must file the entry type 13 data required by CBP electronically in ACE. In addition to the above Entry Type 13 Test data elements, merchandise subject to duties under Chapter 98 or Chapter 99 of the HTSUS, or for which duty-free treatment is claimed under Chapter 98 of the HTSUS or pursuant to a Free Trade Agreement, must transmit the additional data mandated by those requirements, as applicable. Participants with shipments subject to PGA data requirements may also transmit PGA data electronically in ACE with their entry type 13 filing. However, CBP is modifying this test to also temporarily accept transmission of an entry type 13 that is not accompanied by complete electronic PGA data, to allow filers to begin using the entry type 13 while they work to ensure that they can electronically submit all of the data required for complete PGA submissions. CBP will announce the conclusion of this temporary acceptance in a future notice published in the
Federal Register
. For more information on the test procedures and requirements, please refer to the notice announcing the test (
91 FR 38007
) and the CBP and Trade Automated Interface Requirements (CATAIR) guidelines for ACE, which may be found at
https://www.cbp.gov/​trade/​ace/​catair
.

Executive Assistant Commissioner, Office of Trade.

In accordance with the PRA, as part of our
(

continuing effort to reduce paperwork and respondent burdens, we provide the general public and other Federal agencies with an opportunity to comment on new, proposed, revised, and continuing collections of information. This helps us assess the impact of our information collection requirements and minimize the public's reporting burden. We are soliciting comments on the proposed ICR described below. We are especially interested in public comments addressing the following issues:

Abstract:
Respondents to these forms supply the USGS with domestic production and consumption data for 13 ores, concentrates, metals, and ferroalloys, some of which are considered strategic and critical, to assist in determining Defense National Stockpile Center goals. These data and derived information will be published as chapters in USGS Minerals Yearbooks, monthly USGS Mineral Industry Surveys, annual USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries, and special publications for use by Government agencies, Congressional offices, industry education programs, research organizations, financial institutions, consulting firms, industry, academia, and the general public.
The USGS Mineral Resources Program is submitting this
Federal Register
Notice as a revision to add a new `Iron and Steel Scrap and Pig Iron' monthly canvass (USGS Form 9-4148-M) to this ICR and to revise the `Iron and Steel Scrap and Pig Iron' monthly/annual canvass (USGS Form 9-4116-MA) including its conversion to an annual canvass only (USGS Form 9-4116-A). We estimate that the current 30 minutes average estimated burden time for the monthly/annual canvass will decrease to 20 minutes once converted to an annual canvass only. We also estimate an average estimated burden time of 10 minutes for the new `Iron and Steel Scrap and Pig Iron' monthly canvass. These adjustments are designed to boost response rates and maintain essential statistical insights for industry analyses. The annual canvass, in particular, will focus on eliminating redundant data points, allowing for more efficient responses. Both canvasses aim to capture the “missing middle” of scrap consumption—materials sent to manufacturers with scrap and waste materials returned via contract—whereas the previous canvass only identified post-consumer materials and home scrap. The updated form and new form also improve data collection, expand coverage of consumption and production, and support more advanced analytical capabilities.

History
The FAA published an NPRM for Docket No. FAA-2026-9372 in the
Federal Register
(
91 FR 51405

(

; August 13, 2026) to correct a docket number used in two instances. Interested parties were
(
printed page 66637)
invited to participate in this rulemaking effort by submitting written comments on the proposal to the FAA. Two comments were received. One comment expressed support for the NPRM correction.

14 CFR part 71
by establishing Class E airspace extending upward from 700 feet above the surface within a 6.4-mile radius of Mason District Hospital Heliport, Havana, IL. This action is the result of instrument procedures being developed for this heliport to support IFR operations.

under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (
15 U.S.C. 78a
et seq.
) (the “Exchange Act”). The required
Federal Register
notice with a 60-day comment period soliciting comments on this collection of information was published.
[
2
]
In 2010, the Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act (“Dodd-Frank Act”) amended Section 15B of the Exchange Act to require a new class of regulated persons, “municipal advisors,” to register with the Commission.
[
3
]
Section 15B(a)(1)(B) of the Exchange Act, as added by the Dodd-Frank Act, makes it unlawful for a municipal advisor to provide advice to or on behalf of a municipal entity or obligated person with respect to municipal financial products or the issuance of municipal securities, or to undertake certain solicitations of a municipal entity or obligated person, unless the municipal advisor is registered with the Commission.
[
4
]
On September 20, 2013, the Commission adopted Rules 15Ba1-1 through 15Ba1-8 and Rule 15Bc4-1 under the Exchange Act to establish the rules by which a municipal advisor must obtain, maintain, and terminate its registration with the Commission.
[

I. Forms MA and MA-I
Rule 15Ba1-2 requires each person applying for registration with the Commission as a municipal advisor to file electronically with the Commission Form MA and, with respect to each natural person associated with the municipal advisory firm who engages in municipal advisory activities on its behalf, Form MA-I.

9

Rule 15Ba1-5 and the Instructions for the Form MA Series require municipal advisors to amend Form MA annually; amend Form MA whenever certain information previously provided therein becomes inaccurate or materially inaccurate; amend Form MA-I whenever the information previously provided therein becomes inaccurate for any reason; and amend Form MA-I to indicate that an individual is no longer an associated person of the municipal advisory firm filing the form or no longer engaged in municipal advisory activities on its behalf.

Forms MA and MA-I help ensure that the Commission can make information about municipal advisors transparent and easily accessible to the investing public, including municipal entities and obligated persons who engage municipal advisors; investors who may purchase securities from offerings in which municipal advisors participated; and other regulators. Further, the information provided on Forms MA and MA-I expands the amount of publicly available information about municipal advisors and their associated persons, including conflicts of interest and disciplinary history. Although much of the information required by Form MA is already publicly available with respect to municipal advisors that are already registered with the Commission as investment advisers or broker-dealers, many municipal advisors that are not currently registered with the Commission in another capacity will make this information available for the first time. Consequently, the rules and forms allow municipal entities and obligated persons, as well as others, to become more fully informed about municipal advisors in a more efficient manner.
In addition, the requirement that each municipal advisory firm register with the Commission on Form MA and complete Form MA-I with respect to
(
printed page 66759)
each natural person who is a person associated with the municipal advisor and engages in municipal advisory activities on its behalf will help ensure that the Commission has information to oversee respondents and their activities in the municipal securities market effectively. In particular, the information provided in Form MA will be used to determine whether to grant a municipal advisor's application for registration or to institute proceedings to determine whether registration should be denied. The information will also be used to focus examinations and aid in risk-based examinations. Moreover, Forms MA and MA-I will enable the Commission to obtain an accurate estimate of the number of municipal advisors, by size and by municipal advisory activity; analyze data regarding the various types of municipal advisory activities; and evaluate the disciplinary history of all municipal advisors and associated persons, including regulatory, civil, and criminal proceedings.
The requirement that a municipal advisor file amendments to Forms MA and MA-I will help ensure the availability of up-to-date information about municipal advisors and their associated persons.
No assurances of confidentiality are provided with respect to Forms MA and MA-I, except with respect to certain private residential addresses reported therein. Forms MA and MA-I require applicants and registered municipal advisors to report various addresses, which may include private residential addresses. However, where the forms request an address, the applicant or registrant is asked to indicate whether the address provided is a private residence and is advised that, if so, the private residential address will not be included in publicly available versions of the form.

ACTION:

SUMMARY:
In accordance with the Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act (NAGPRA), the Rhode Island School of Design, Museum of Art (RISD), intends to repatriate certain cultural items that meet the definition of sacred objects/objects of cultural patrimony and that have a cultural affiliation with the Indian Tribes or

Native Hawaiian organizations in this notice.
DATES:
Repatriation of the cultural items in this notice may occur on or after November 23, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
Send additional, written requests for repatriation of the cultural items in this notice to Joe Leduc, Museum of Art, Rhode Island School of Design, 20 North Main Street, Providence, RI 02903, email
jleduc@risd.edu
, or María Fernanda Mancera, Museum of Art, Rhode Island School of Design, 20 North Main Street, Providence, RI 02903, email
mmancera@risd.edu
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
This notice is published as part of the National Park Service's administrative responsibilities under NAGPRA. The determinations in this notice are the sole responsibility of the RISD and additional information on the determinations in this notice, including the results of consultation, can be found in the summary or related records. The National Park Service is not responsible for the determinations in this notice.
Abstract of Information Available
A total of 11 cultural items have been requested for repatriation. The 11 sacred objects/objects of cultural patriomony are
kapa
, traditional barkcloth—non-woven textiles—made by Kanaka Maoli (Indigenous Hawaiians). Six of the cultural items were given to RISD, by Brown University in 1922. The remaining five were added to the collection in the 1990s. One has unclear provenance, one was a gift from Mr. Gustav Radeke, and three were given by Lillian M. Potter. There is no known treatment of the
kapa
with potentially hazardous substances.
Determinations
The RISD has determined that:
The 11 sacred objects/objects of cultural patrimony described in this notice are, according to the Native American traditional knowledge of an Indian Tribe or Native Hawaiian organization, specific ceremonial objects needed by a traditional Native American religious leader for present-day adherents to practice traditional Native American religion, and have ongoing historical, traditional, or cultural importance central to the Native American group, including any constituent sub-group (such as a band, clan, lineage, ceremonial society, or other subdivision).
There is a connection between the cultural items described in this notice and the Hui Iwi Kuamo`o.
Requests for Repatriation
Additional, written requests for repatriation of the cultural items in this notice must be sent to the authorized representative identified in this notice under
ADDRESSES
. Requests for repatriation may be submitted by any lineal descendant, Indian Tribe, or Native Hawaiian organization not identified in this notice who shows, by a preponderance of the evidence, that the requestor is a lineal descendant or a culturally affiliated Indian Tribe or Native Hawaiian organization.
Repatriation of the cultural items in this notice to a requestor may occur on or after November 23, 2026. If competing requests for repatriation are received, the Museum of Art, Rhode Island School of Design must determine the most appropriate requestor prior to repatriation. Requests for joint repatriation of the cultural items are considered a single request and not competing requests. The Museum of Art, Rhode Island School of Design is responsible for sending a copy of this notice to the Indian Tribes and Native Hawaiian organizations identified in this notice and to any other consulting parties.
Authority:
Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act,
25 U.S.C. 3004
and the implementing regulations,
43 CFR 10.9
.

Abstract of Information Available
A total of one lot of cultural items have been requested for repatriation. The one lot of unassociated funerary objects are faunal bone, shell, lithics, pottery, ochre, sediment samples, and fossils. The cultural items were removed from the Fisher site (11WI0005) in Will County, Illinois in circa 1946-1950 under the direction of George R. Horner of Wheaton College. The Horner investigations focused on the house pit 48 area. The collection dates to approximately A.D. 800-1400 and the late 17th century. No hazardous substances are known to have been used to treat any of the cultural items.
Determinations
The University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee has determined that:
The one lot of unassociated funerary objects described in this notice are reasonably believed to have been placed intentionally with or near human remains, and are connected, either at the time of death or later as part of the death rite or ceremony of a Native American culture according to the Native American traditional knowledge of a lineal descendant, Indian Tribe, or Native Hawaiian organization. The unassociated funerary objects have been identified by a preponderance of the evidence as related to human remains, specific individuals, or families, or removed from a specific burial site or burial area of an individual or individuals with cultural affiliation to an Indian Tribe or Native Hawaiian organization.
There is a connection between the cultural items described in this notice and the Ho-Chunk Nation of Wisconsin.

[N7582; NPS-WASO-NAGPRA-NPS0044033; PPWOCRADN0-PCU00RP14.R50000]
AGENCY:
National Park Service, Interior.
ACTION:
Notice.
SUMMARY:
In accordance with the Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act (NAGPRA), the University of Kansas has completed an inventory of human remains and has determined that there is a cultural affiliation between the human remains and Indian Tribes or Native Hawaiian organizations in this notice.
DATES:
Repatriation of the human remains in this notice may occur on or after November 23, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
Send written requests for repatriation of the human remains in this notice to John Curran, University of Kansas, Office of Audit, Risk & Compliance, 1450 Jayhawk Blvd., 345 Strong Hall, Lawrence, KS 66045, email
repatriation@ku.edu
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
This notice is published as part of the National Park Service's administrative responsibilities under NAGPRA. The determinations in this notice are the sole responsibility of the University of Kansas and additional information on the determinations in this notice, including the results of consultation, can be found in its inventory or related records. The National Park Service is not responsible for the determinations in this notice.
Abstract of Information Available
Human remains representing at least one individual have been identified. No associated funerary objects are present. The remains, a scalp, were transferred to the University of Kansas on June 7, 1956. It had been sent to the university by Alexander Rankin of Mission, Kansas, possibly a descendant of the original collector, also named Alexander Rankin. According to provenance records, the scalp was reportedly taken by the Osage in a raid on a Plains Tribe. An Osage Chief gave the scalp to Alexander Rankin around 1872. Rankin, a U.S. Licensed Indian Trader with the
(
printed page 66728)
Sac and Fox Tribe of Quenemo, Kansas, had opened a trading post in 1872 at the Osage Agency, present-day Pawhuska, Oklahoma. There are no known chemical treatments to the human remains.
Cultural Affiliation
Based on the information available and the results of consultation, cultural affiliation is reasonably identified by the geographical location or acquisition history of the human remains described in this notice.
Determinations
The University of Kansas has determined that:
The human remains described in this notice represent the physical remains of one individual of Native American ancestry.
There is a connection between the human remains described in this notice and The Osage Nation.
Requests for Repatriation
Written requests for repatriation of the human remains in this notice must be sent to the authorized representative identified in this notice under
ADDRESSES
. Requests for repatriation may be submitted by:
1. Any one or more of the Indian Tribes or Native Hawaiian organizations identified in this notice.
2. Any lineal descendant, Indian Tribe, or Native Hawaiian organization not identified in this notice who shows, by a preponderance of the evidence, that the requestor is a lineal descendant or an Indian Tribe or Native Hawaiian organization with cultural affiliation.
Repatriation of the human remains described in this notice to a requestor may occur on or after November 23, 2026. If competing requests for repatriation are received, the University of Kansas must determine the most appropriate requestor prior to repatriation. Requests for joint repatriation of the human remains are considered a single request and not competing requests. The University of Kansas is responsible for sending a copy of this notice to the Indian Tribes and Native Hawaiian organizations identified in this notice and any other consulting parties.
Authority:
Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act,
25 U.S.C. 3003
, and the implementing regulations,
43 CFR 10.10
.
Dated: October 15, 2026.
Melanie O'Brien,
Manager, National NAGPRA Program.

Filed 10-21-26; 8:45 am]

AGENCY:
National Park Service, Interior.
ACTION:
Notice.
SUMMARY:
In accordance with the Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act (NAGPRA), Boston University (BU) has completed an inventory of human remains and associated funerary objects and has determined that there is a cultural affiliation between the human remains and associated funerary objects and Indian Tribes or Native Hawaiian organizations in this notice.
DATES:
Repatriation of the human remains and associated funerary objects in this notice may occur on or after November 23, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
Send written requests for repatriation of the human remains and associated funerary objects in this notice to Kathryn M. Mellouk, Associate Vice President for Research Compliance, Boston University, One Silber Way, 9th Floor, Boston, MA 02215, email
kateski@bu.edu
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
This notice is published as part of the National Park Service's administrative responsibilities under NAGPRA. The determinations in this notice are the sole responsibility of BU, and additional information on the determinations in this notice, including the results of consultation, can be found in its inventory or related records. The National Park Service is not responsible for the determinations in this notice.
Abstract of Information Available
Human remains representing at least four individuals have been identified. Based on the information available, four lots of associated funerary objects are present. These are represented by one lot porcelain and ceramic fragments, one lot nails and screws; one lot slag, and one lot mixed materials including soil. On an unknown date the human remains and associated funerary objects were removed from Beverly, Essex County, Massachusetts by an unknown individual. In October 2024 the human remains and associated funerary objects were identified during an archaeological collections assessment of the now defunct Boston University Office of Public Archaeology repository.
Cultural Affiliation
Based on the information available and the results of consultation, cultural affiliation is reasonably identified by the geographical location or acquisition history of the associated funerary objects described in this notice.
Determinations
BU has determined that:
The human remains described in this notice represent the physical remains of four individuals of Native American ancestry.
The four lots of objects described in this notice are reasonably believed to have been placed intentionally with or near individual human remains at the time of death or later as part of the death rite or ceremony.
There is a reasonable connection between the associated funerary objects described in this notice and the Houlton Band of Maliseet Indians; Mashantucket Pequot Indian Tribe; Mashpee Wampanoag Tribe; Mi'kmaq Nation (previously listed as Aroostook Band of Micmacs); Mohegan Tribe of Indians of Connecticut; Narragansett Indian Tribe; Passamaquoddy Tribe; Penobscot Nation; and the Wampanoag Tribe of Gay Head (Aquinnah).
Requests for Repatriation
Written requests for repatriation of the human remains and associated funerary objects in this notice must be sent to the authorized representative identified in this notice under
ADDRESSES
. Requests for repatriation may be submitted by:
1. Any one or more of the Indian Tribes or Native Hawaiian organizations identified in this notice.
2. Any lineal descendant, Indian Tribe, or Native Hawaiian organization not identified in this notice who shows, by a preponderance of the evidence, that the requestor is a lineal descendant or an Indian Tribe or Native Hawaiian organization with cultural affiliation.
Repatriation of the human remains and associated funerary objects described in this notice to a requestor may occur on or after November 23, 2026. If competing requests for repatriation are received, BU must determine the most appropriate requestor prior to repatriation. Requests for joint repatriation of the human remains and associated funerary objects are considered a single request and not competing requests. BU is responsible for sending a copy of this notice to the Indian Tribes and Native Hawaiian organizations identified in this notice and any other consulting parties.
Authority:
Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act,
25 U.S.C. 3003
, and the implementing regulations,
43 CFR 10.10
.
Dated: October 15, 2026.

Manager, National NAGPRA Program.

Department of Commerce
Foreign-Trade Zones Board
[B-138-2026]
Metal Container (MCC) LP submitted a notification of proposed production activity to the FTZ Board (the Board) for its facility in Windsor, Colorado within FTZ 123. The notification conforming to the requirements of the Board's regulations (
15 CFR 400.22
) was received on September 30, 2026.
Pursuant to
15 CFR 400.14(b)
, FTZ production activity would be limited to the specific foreign-status material/component and specific finished product described in the submitted notification (summarized below) and subsequently authorized by the Board. The benefits that may stem from conducting production activity under FTZ procedures are explained in the background section of the Board's website—accessible via
www.trade.gov/​ftz
.
The proposed finished product is empty beverage cans (body only) (duty rate 5.7%).
The proposed foreign-status material/component is aluminum body stock (duty rate 3%).
The request indicates that aluminum stock is subject to duties under section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962 (section 232) and section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 (section 301),
(
printed page 66671)
depending on the country of origin. The applicable section 232 and section 301 decisions require subject merchandise to be admitted to FTZs in privileged foreign status (
19 CFR 146.41
).
Public comment is invited from interested parties. Submissions shall be addressed to the Board's Executive Secretary and sent to:
ftz@trade.gov
. The closing period for their receipt is December 1, 2026.
A copy of the notification will be available for public inspection in the “Online FTZ Information System” section of the Board's website.
For further information, contact Christopher Wedderburn at
Chris.Wedderburn@trade.gov
.
Dated: October 16, 2026.

Executive Secretary.

AGENCY:
National Park Service, Interior.
ACTION:
Notice.
SUMMARY:
In accordance with the Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act (NAGPRA), the U.S. Department of the Interior, Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA) and the Museum of Northern Arizona University has completed an inventory of human remains and associated funerary objects and has determined that there is a cultural affiliation between the human remains and associated funerary objects and Indian Tribes or Native Hawaiian organizations in this notice.
DATES:
Repatriation of the human remains and associated funerary objects in this notice may occur on or after November 23, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
Send written requests for repatriation of the human remains and associated funerary objects in this notice to Tamara Billie, U.S. Department of Interior, Bureau of Indian Affairs, Office of Trust Services, Division of Environmental Services and Cultural Resources Management, 1001 Indian School Road NW, Mailbox 44, Albuquerque, NM 87104, email
tamara.billie@bia.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
This notice is published as part of the National Park Service's administrative responsibilities under NAGPRA. The determinations in this notice are the sole responsibility of the BIA, and additional information on the determinations in this notice, including the results of consultation, can be found
(
printed page 66723)
in its inventory or related records. The National Park Service is not responsible for the determinations in this notice.
Abstract of Information Available
Human remains representing at least six individuals have been identified from NA897, Long House Pueblo. The 73 associated funerary objects are six ceramic vessels, two unfired ceramic vessels, 50 ceramic sherds, one faunal bone tool, 13 rocks, and one soil sample. Potentially hazardous substances are present on three of the individuals, which were treated with PVA dissolved in ethyl alcohol applied directly to the bones. The site was excavated in 1967 and 1969 by the Museum of Northern Arizona (MNA) during an authorized project to address human remains eroding from the midden. Funerary objects from this site (ceramic sherds and rocks) believed to be from the 1969 excavations and found at Northern Arizona University were transferred to MNA for repatriation and are included in the above counts. The site is at the northern end of Long House Valley, Navajo County, Arizona.
Human remains representing at least six individuals have been identified from NA1292. No associated funerary objects are present. Potentially hazardous substances are present on two of the individuals, which were treated with PVA dissolved in ethyl alcohol applied directly to the bones. The site was excavated in 1935 during an MNA expedition. The site is near Grand Falls overlooking the Little Colorado River, Coconino County, Arizona.
Human remains representing at least four individuals have been identified from NA1600. The 408 associated funerary objects are 21 ceramic vessels; one worked ceramic sherd; one necklace made of shell, stone, and turquoise beads; one mano; one mano fragment; one head stone; one hand stone; 380 ceramic sherds; and one vegetal sample. Potentially hazardous substances are present on four of the individuals, which were treated with PVA dissolved in ethyl alcohol applied directly to the bones. The site was excavated in 1935 during an MNA expedition. The site is near Grand Falls, Coconino County, Arizona.
Human remains representing, at least three individuals have been identified from NA2521, Turkey House. The 129 associated funerary objects are one ceramic disc fragment, 125 ceramic sherds and three faunal bones. Potentially hazardous substances are present on one individual, which was treated with PVA dissolved in ethyl alcohol applied directly to the bones. Individuals were collected from the surface of the site in 1968 by MNA during an authorized project. The site is in Tsegi Canyon, Navajo County, Arizona.
Human remains representing at least, one individual has been identified from NA2526. No associated funerary objects are present. No known hazardous materials are present. The individual was exposed on the surface of the site and collected in 1934 during MNA's fieldwork associated with the Rainbow Bridge—Monument Valley Expedition. The site is near Marsh Pass, Navajo County, Arizona.
Human remains representing, at least, one individual have been identified from NA2537, Turkey House. The 39 associated funerary objects are one stone bead, one ceramic disc fragment, 33 ceramic sherds, three faunal bone, and one vegetal sample. No known hazardous materials are present. The individual was exposed on the surface of the site and collected in 1934 during MNA's fieldwork associated with the Rainbow Bridge—Monument Valley Expedition. The site is near Marsh Pass, Navajo County, Arizona.
Human remains representing at least, one individual has been identified from NA2590. No associated funerary objects are present. Potentially hazardous substances are present on this individual, which was treated with PVA dissolved in ethyl alcohol applied directly to the bones. The site was recorded in 1934 during an MNA expedition, and the individual was probably collected at this time. The site is near the town of Pinyon, Navajo County, Arizona.
Human remains representing at least, one individual has been identified from NA2644. No associated funerary objects are present. No known hazardous materials are present. The site was recorded in 1933 during the National Park Monument Valley Expedition, who was working with the Rainbow Bridge—Monument Valley Expedition. The individual was identified during inventory of faunal remains at MNA. The site is east of Navajo Mountain, Coconino County, Arizona.
Human remains representing, at least, one individual have been identified from NA2721, Slab House. No associated funerary objects are present. No known hazardous materials are present. The site was visited by MNA in 1963 to recover human remains eroding from the site. The site is in a tributary of Oljato Wash, Navajo County, Arizona.
Human remains representing at least 22 individuals have been identified from NA3112, Woodchuck Cave. The 427 associated funerary objects are three bundles of human hair, three human hair cordage fragments, three cordage fragments with human hair, two basket fragments with human hair, one sandal fragment with human hair, two coprolites, 17 cordage fragments (fiber and fiber with beads, fur, feather, stick), three fiber fragments (yucca and sinew), 11 basket fragments, six sandal fragments, three cloth fragments, one hair ornament (wood, animal hide, agave cordage), two comb fragments (wood, shell, stone), two fur robe fragments, 11 feathers, nine animal hide and fur fragments, one animal feces sample, two stone pendants, nine stone and shell pendants, 12 beads (stone and shell), three necklaces (acorn and yucca, shell, stone and shell), nine wooden gaming pieces, three atlatl fragments (wood, animal hide, antler), one wood mortar with pigment, five faunal bone tools (awl, flaking tool), 10 faunal bone beads, three faunal bone dice, seven projectile points, one stone spindle whorl/disc, one stone sphere, four stone manos, two stone abraders, two pieces of unfired pottery, one clay pipe, one stone pipe, one stone pipe with bead, six flaked stone, 17 faunal bones, 212 seeds, four mineral samples, 17 pigment samples, seven pieces of wood, six vegetal samples, and one insect. Potentially hazardous substances are present on one individual, which was treated with PVA dissolved in ethyl alcohol applied directly to the bones. The site was excavated in 1934 by MNA during work related to the Rainbow Bridge—Monument Valley Expedition. The site is southwest of Kayenta, Navajo County, Arizona.

The site is near Marsh Pass, Navajo County, Arizona.

The 27 associated funerary objects are six stone beads, two stone pendants, one soil sample, and 18 ceramic sherds. No known hazardous materials are present. The site was recorded by MNA in 1976 during an authorized service project to document and remove exposed human remains. The site is in Marsh Pass, Navajo County, Arizona.
Human remains representing at least, one individual has been identified from NA10548. The 113 associated funerary objects are 110 ceramic sherds and three ground stone. No known hazardous materials are present. The site was partially excavated by MNA in 1968 during an authorized project to address human remains eroding out of the site. The site is in Marsh Pass, Navajo County, Arizona.
Human remains representing at least two individuals have been identified from NA10549. The 67 associated funerary objects are three ceramic sherds, 63 ceramic sherds, and one vegetal sample. No known hazardous materials are present. The site was partially excavated by MNA in 1968 during an authorized project to address human remains eroding out of the site. The site is in Kiet Siel Canyon, Navajo County, Arizona.
Human remains representing, at least, three individuals have been identified from NA10554. The three associated funerary objects are one ceramic vessel, one sample of wood, and one vegetal sample. No known hazardous materials are present. The site was partially excavated by MNA in 1968 during an authorized project to address human remains eroding from an arroyo. The site is in Long House Valley, Navajo County, Arizona.
Human remains representing at least, one individual has been identified from NA10753. The 80 associated funerary objects are 77 ceramic sherds, two rocks, and one soil sample. No known hazardous materials are present. The site was partially excavated by MNA in 1970 during an authorized project to address human remains eroding from a drainage. The site is near the old Tsegi Trading Post, Navajo County, Arizona.
Human remains representing at least three individuals have been identified from NA10757. The 75 associated funerary objects are 68 ceramic sherds and seven flaked stones. No known hazardous materials are present. The site was recorded and excavated by MNA in 1970 during an authorized compliance project along BIA Route 15. The site is near Dilkon, Navajo County, Arizona.

ceramic sherds, and six soil samples. No known hazardous materials are present. The site was partially excavated by MNA in 1970 during an authorized project to address exposed human remains at the site. The site is near the community of Inscription House, Coconino County, Arizona.
Human remains representing at least, one individual has been identified from NA11141. The one associated funerary object is a ceramic vessel. No known hazardous materials are present. Human remains representing at least, one individual has been identified from NA11963. No associated funerary objects are present. No known hazardous materials are present. Human remains representing at least three individuals have been identified from NA12063. The one associated funerary object is vegetal material. No known hazardous materials are present. Human remains representing at least, one individual has been identified from NA13921. No associated funerary objects are present. No known hazardous materials are present. Human remains representing at least, one individual has been identified from NA14193. The 23 associated funerary objects are 10 ceramic vessels, seven faunal bone, two flaked stone, two mineral samples, and two soil samples. No known hazardous materials are present. The site was recorded by MNA in 1974 for an authorized project to address human remains eroding out of a road-cut resulting from the construction along Navajo Route 15. The site is near Dilkon, Navajo County, Arizona.
Human remains representing, at least, one individual have been identified from AZ-J-54-7 (NN). No associated funerary objects are present. No known hazardous materials are present. The site was excavated by the Navajo Nation Cultural Resource Management Program in 1979 during an authorized project along the proposed BIA Route N41 corridor. The site is near Pinon, Navajo County, Arizona.
Human remains representing at least four individuals have been identified from AZ-J-54-9 (NN). The five associated funerary objects are ceramic vessels. No known hazardous materials are present. The site was excavated by the Navajo Nation Cultural Resource Management Program in 1979 during an authorized project along the proposed BIA Route N41 corridor. The site is near Pinon, Navajo County, Arizona.
Cultural Affiliation
Based on the information available and the results of consultation, cultural affiliation is reasonably identified by the geographical location or acquisition history of the human remains and associated funerary objects described in this notice.
Determinations
The BIA has determined that:
The human remains described in this notice represent the physical remains of 139 individuals of Native American ancestry.
The 2,222 objects described in this notice are reasonably believed to have been placed intentionally with or near individual human remains at the time of death or later as part of the death rite or ceremony.
There is a connection between the human remains and associated funerary objects described in this notice and the Navajo Nation, Arizona, New Mexico, & Utah.
Requests for Repatriation
Written requests for repatriation of the human remains and associated funerary objects in this notice must be sent to the authorized representative identified in this notice under
ADDRESSES
. Requests for repatriation may be submitted by:
1. Any one or more of the Indian Tribes or Native Hawaiian organizations identified in this notice.
2. Any lineal descendant, Indian Tribe, or Native Hawaiian organization not identified in this notice who shows, by a preponderance of the evidence, that the requestor is a lineal descendant or an Indian Tribe or Native Hawaiian organization with cultural affiliation.
Repatriation of the human remains and associated funerary objects described in this notice to a requestor may occur on or after November 23, 2026. If competing requests for repatriation are received, the BIA must determine the most appropriate requestor prior to repatriation. Requests for joint repatriation of the human remains and associated funerary objects are considered a single request and not competing requests. The BIA is responsible for sending a copy of this notice to the Indian Tribes and Native Hawaiian organizations identified in this notice and any other consulting parties.

ACTION:
Notice.
SUMMARY:
In accordance with the Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act (NAGPRA), Fernbank Museum of Natural History has completed an inventory of human remains and has determined that there is a cultural affiliation between the human remains and Indian Tribes or Native Hawaiian organizations in this notice.
DATES:
Repatriation of the human remains in this notice may occur on or after November 23, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
Send written requests for repatriation of the human remains in this notice to Wil Grewe-Mullins, Fernbank Museum of Natural History, 767 Clifton Road NE, Atlanta, GA 30307, email
Wil.Grewe-Mullins@fernbankmuseum.org
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
This notice is published as part of the National Park Service's administrative responsibilities under NAGPRA. The determinations in this notice are the sole responsibility of the Fernbank Museum of Natural History, and additional information on the determinations in this notice, including the results of consultation, can be found in its inventory or related records. The National Park Service is not responsible for the determinations in this notice.
Abstract of Information Available
Human remains representing at least one individual have been identified. No associated funerary objects are present. The ancestors were recovered from 9LI66, Walburg Creek (AMNH 385), on St. Catherines Island in Liberty County, Georgia. These materials were recovered from two test pits during archaeological excavations conducted in the 1970s by the American Museum of Natural History under the direction of Dr. David Hurst Thomas. The remains were subsequently subjected to bioarcheological study under the direction of Dr. Clark S. Larsen, working in collaboration with the American Museum of Natural History. After storage for intervals at the American Museum of Natural History and on St. Catherines Island, the remains and funerary objects were transferred in 2004 to Fernbank Museum of Natural History by the St. Catherines Island and Edward John Noble Foundations. There is no evidence of any potentially hazardous substances used to treat any of the human remains.
Human remains representing at least 15 individuals have been identified. No associated funerary objects are present. The ancestors were recovered from 9Li74, Santa Catalina de Guale Mission cemetery, on St. Catherines Island in Liberty County, Georgia. The materials were recovered during archaeological excavations under the direction of Dr. David Hurst Thomas and Dr. Clark Larsen, working in collaboration with the American Museum of Natural History. The remains represent small quantities of highly fragmented bone and ash that were sent to the University of Wisconsin—Madison for isotopic analysis and recently integrated into the collection at Fernbank. There is no evidence of any potentially hazardous substances used to treat any of the human remains.
Human remains representing at least two individuals have been identified. No associated funerary objects are present. The ancestors were identified in collections with no context or provenience other than they were recovered from St. Catherines Island in Liberty County, Georgia. The materials would have been recovered during archaeological excavations conducted by the American Museum of Natural History under the direction of Dr. David Hurst Thomas. The remains were likely subjected to bioarcheological study under the direction of Dr. Clark S. Larsen, working in collaboration with the American Museum of Natural History. After storage for intervals at the American Museum of Natural History and on St. Catherines Island, the remains were transferred in 2004 to Fernbank Museum of Natural History by the St. Catherines Island and Edward John Noble Foundations. There is no evidence of any potentially hazardous substances used to treat any of the human remains.
Cultural Affiliation
Based on the information available and the results of consultation, cultural affiliation is reasonably identified by the geographical location and acquisition history of the human remains described in this notice.
Determinations
The Fernbank Museum of Natural History has determined that:
The human remains described in this notice represent the physical remains of at least 18 individuals of Native American ancestry.
There is a connection between the human remains described in this notice and the Alabama-Quassarte Tribal Town; Miccosukee Tribe of Indians; Poarch Band of Creek Indians; Seminole Tribe of Florida; The Muscogee (Creek) Nation; The Seminole Nation of Oklahoma; and the Thlopthlocco Tribal Town.
Requests for Repatriation
Written requests for repatriation of the human remains in this notice must be sent to the authorized representative identified in this notice under
ADDRESSES
. Requests for repatriation may be submitted by:
1. Any one or more of the Indian Tribes or Native Hawaiian organizations identified in this notice.
2. Any lineal descendant, Indian Tribe, or Native Hawaiian organization not identified in this notice who shows, by a preponderance of the evidence, that the requestor is a lineal descendant or an Indian Tribe or Native Hawaiian organization with cultural affiliation.
Repatriation of the human remains described in this notice to a requestor may occur on or after November 23, 2026. If competing requests for repatriation are received, the Fernbank Museum of Natural History must determine the most appropriate requestor prior to repatriation. Requests for joint repatriation of the human remains are considered a single request

AGENCY:
National Park Service, Interior.
ACTION:
Notice.
SUMMARY:
In accordance with the Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act (NAGPRA), the Sonoma State University intends to repatriate certain cultural items that meet the definition of objects of cultural patrimony and that have a cultural affiliation with the Indian Tribes or Native Hawaiian organizations in this notice.
DATES:
Repatriation of the cultural items in this notice may occur on or after November 23, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
Send additional, written requests for repatriation of the cultural items in this notice to Kirsten Twork, Sonoma State University, 1801 E Cotati Avenue, Rohnert Park, CA 94928, email
tworkk@sonoma.edu
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
This notice is published as part of the National Park Service's administrative responsibilities under NAGPRA. The determinations in this notice are the sole responsibility of the Sonoma State University, and additional information on the determinations in this notice, including the results of consultation, can be found in the summary or related records. The National Park Service is not responsible for the determinations in this notice.
Abstract of Information Available
A total of 374 lots of cultural items have been requested for repatriation. The 374 lots of objects of cultural patrimony include modified stone, faunal bone, unmodified stone, and historics.
In 2010 CA-NEV-1842, CA-NEV-1843, and CA-NEV-2066 were investigated by the Anthropological Studies Center of Sonoma State University.
Determinations
The Sonoma State University has determined that:
The 374 lots of objects of cultural patrimony described in this notice have ongoing historical, traditional, or cultural importance central to the Native American group, including any constituent sub-group (such as a band, clan, lineage, ceremonial society, or other subdivision), according to the Native American traditional knowledge of an Indian Tribe or Native Hawaiian organization.
There is a connection between the cultural items described in this notice and the United Auburn Indian Community of the Auburn Rancheria of California.
Requests for Repatriation
Additional, written requests for repatriation of the cultural items in this notice must be sent to the authorized representative identified in this notice under
ADDRESSES
. Requests for repatriation may be submitted by any lineal descendant, Indian Tribe, or Native Hawaiian organization not identified in this notice who shows, by a preponderance of the evidence, that the requestor is a lineal descendant or a culturally affiliated Indian Tribe or Native Hawaiian organization.
Repatriation of the cultural items in this notice to a requestor may occur on or after November 23, 2026. If competing requests for repatriation are received, the Sonoma State University must determine the most appropriate requestor prior to repatriation. Requests for joint repatriation of the cultural items are considered a single request and not competing requests. The Sonoma State University is responsible for sending a copy of this notice to the Indian Tribes and Native Hawaiian organizations identified in this notice and to any other consulting parties.
Authority:
Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act,
25 U.S.C. 3004
and the implementing regulations,
43 CFR 10.9
.
(
printed page 66722)
Dated: October 15, 2026.
Melanie O'Brien,
Manager, National NAGPRA Program.

SUMMARY:
In accordance with the Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act (NAGPRA), the Autry Museum of the American West (Southwest Museum of the American Indian Collection) intends to repatriate certain cultural items that meet the definition of unassociated funerary objects, sacred objects, and/or objects of cultural patrimony and that have a cultural affiliation with the Indian Tribes or Native Hawaiian organizations in this notice.
DATES:
Repatriation of the cultural items in this notice may occur on or after November 23, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
Send additional, written requests for repatriation of the cultural items in this notice to Karimah Richardson, M.Phil., RPA, Associate Curator of Anthropology and Repatriation Supervisor, Autry Museum of the American West, 4700 Western Heritage Way, Los Angeles, CA 90027, email
krichardson@theautry.org
.

This notice is published as part of the National Park Service's administrative responsibilities under NAGPRA. The determinations in this notice are the sole responsibility of the Autry Museum of the American West, and additional information on the determinations in this notice, including the results of consultation, can be found in the summary or related records. The National Park Service is not responsible for the determinations in this notice.
Abstract of Information Available
El Dorado County
A total of one cultural item has been requested for repatriation. The one object of cultural patrimony is a large ground stone. On an unknown date, Max Fisher collected the cultural item from an unknown site in Placerville, El Dorado County, CA. Mrs. Bertha H. Heise donated the cultural material to the Southwest Museum of the American Indian (now a part of the Autry Museum of the American West) in 1948.
Sacramento County
A total of 10 lots of cultural items has been requested for repatriation. The 10 lots of unassociated funerary objects are 10 lots of lithics. On an unknown date, the cultural material was collected from Thistle Mound, Sacramento, Sacramento County, CA by the Sacramento Junior College Field Party. College President Jeremiah B. Lillard donated the cultural materials to the Southwest Museum in 1935.
A total of two cultural items has been requested for repatriation. The two unassociated funerary objects are two ground stone objects. Sometime in 1931, Mr. Henry Gibbs and Sacramento Junior College President Mr. Jeremiah B. Lillard, as part of the Sacramento Junior College Field Party, collected the cultural material from CA-SAC-122 in Sacramento County, CA. College President Jeremiah B. Lillard donated the cultural materials to the Southwest Museum in 1935.
A total of six lots of cultural items have been requested for repatriation. The six lots of unassociated funerary objects are six lots of worked shell. On an unknown date, an unknown collector collected the cultural materials from an unknown mound along the American River in Sacramento County, CA. Mr. John George Braecklein donated the cultural materials to the Southwest Museum in 1943.
A total of 26 lots of cultural items has been requested for repatriation. The 26 lots of unassociated funerary objects are 18 baked clay objects, two lots of lithics, two ground stones, and four lots of worked shell. In 1931, the Sacramento Junior College Field Party, Mr. Henry Gibbs, and college president Mr. Jeremiah B. Lillard collected the cultural materials from CA-SAC-6 in Sacramento County, CA. College President Jeremiah B. Lillard donated the cultural materials to the Southwest Museum in 1935.
A total of two cultural items has been requested for repatriation. The two unassociated funerary objects are one worked faunal bone fragment and one baked clay object. In 1933, Sacramento Junior College President Mr. Jeremiah B. Lillard, as part of the Sacramento Junior College Field Party, collected the cultural material from CA-SAC-29 in Sacramento County, CA. College President Jeremiah B. Lillard donated the cultural materials to the Southwest Museum in 1935.
A total of 29 lots of cultural items has been requested for repatriation. The 29 lots of unassociated funerary objects are 14 lots of lithics, six lots of worked faunal bones, four lots of worked shell, four ground stones, and one lot of worked stone. In 1931, Mr. Henry Gibbs, as part of the Sacramento Junior College Field Party, collected the cultural materials from CA-SAC-16 in Sacramento County, CA. College President Jeremiah B. Lillard donated the cultural materials to the Southwest Museum in 1935.
A total of one lot of cultural items have been requested for repatriation. The one lot of unassociated funerary objects is one lot of worked shell. On an unknown date, collector and donor Mr. John George Braecklein collected the cultural materials from CA-SAC-16 in Sacramento County, CA. Mr. Braecklein donated the cultural materials to the Southwest Museum in 1947.
A total of one cultural item has been requested for repatriation. The one unassociated funerary object is one worked faunal object. In 1931, Sacramento Junior College President Mr. Jeremiah B. Lillard, as part of the Sacramento Junior College Field Party, collected the cultural item from CA-SAC-64 in Sacramento County, CA. College President Jeremiah B. Lillard donated the cultural materials to the Southwest Museum in 1935.
A total of one lot of cultural items has been requested for repatriation. The one lot of unassociated funerary objects are one lot of worked shell. On an unknown date, an unknown collector collected the cultural materials from an unknown site in Sacramento, Sacramento County, CA. Mr. John George Braecklein donated the cultural materials to the Southwest Museum in 1943.
A total of four lots of cultural items has been requested for repatriation. The four lots of unassociated funerary objects are four lots of ornaments. On an unknown date, an unknown collector collected the cultural materials from an unknown site in Sacramento, Sacramento County, CA. Mrs. Louisa W. Hutchinson donated the cultural
(
