materials to the Southwest Museum in 1947.
A total of one cultural item has been requested for repatriation. The one unassociated funerary object is one sandstone ground stone. On an unknown date, an unknown collector collected the cultural item from an unknown site in Sacramento, Sacramento County, CA. Mr. Hubert H. Weiser donated the cultural material to the Southwest Museum in 1986.
A total of one cultural item has been requested for repatriation. The one unassociated funerary object is one ground stone. In 1933, Mr. Robert F. Heizer collected the cultural item from CA-SAC-73 in Sacramento County, CA. Mr. Heizer donated the cultural material to the Southwest Museum in 1938.
A total of one cultural item has been requested for repatriation. The one unassociated funerary object is one modified faunal bone tool. In 1931, Mr. Henry Gibb and the Sacramento Junior College Field Party collected the cultural item from CA-SAC-21 in Sacramento County, CA. College president Mr. Jeremiah B. Lillard donated the cultural material to the Southwest Museum in 1935.
A total of one lot of cultural items has been requested for repatriation. The one lot of unassociated funerary objects are one lot of worked shell. On an unknown date, Mr. Harry Brisley collected the cultural items from CA-SAC-21 in Sacramento County, CA. Mr. Brisley donated the cultural materials to the Southwest Museum in 1947.
A total of one lot of cultural items has been requested for repatriation. The one lot of unassociated funerary objects are one lot of worked shells. On an unknown date, an unknown collector collected the cultural items from an unknown site near Sutter's Fort in Sacramento County, CA. Mr. John George Braecklein donated the cultural materials to the Southwest Museum in 1943.
A total of one cultural item has been requested for repatriation. The one unassociated funerary object is one worked faunal bone tool. In 1933, Sacramento Junior College President Mr. Jeremiah B. Lillard, as part of the Sacramento Junior College Field Party, collected the cultural item from CA-SAC-28, in Sacramento County, CA. Mr. Lillard donated the cultural material to the Southwest Museum in 1935.
A total of two cultural items have been requested for repatriation. The two unassociated funerary objects are two lithics. On an unknown date, Mr. Fredrick Hastings Rindge collected the cultural items from an unknown site near Sacramento in Sacramento County, CA. Mr. Rindge's daughter, Mrs. Rhoda Rindge Adamson, donated the cultural materials to the Southwest Museum in 1943.
A total of two lots of cultural items has been requested for repatriation. The two lots of unassociated funerary objects are two lots of worked shell. On an unknown date, Mr. Henry Brisley collected the cultural items from an unknown site near Sacramento in Sacramento County, CA. Mr. Brisley donated the cultural materials to the Southwest Museum in 1947.
Yolo County
A total of one cultural item has been requested for repatriation. The one unassociated funerary object is one worked stone. On an unknown date, Mr. Harold E. Murdock collected the cultural item from CA-YOL-13 in Yolo County, CA. Mr. Hubert H. Weiser donated the cultural material to the Southwest Museum in 1986.
Sacramento Valley
A total of one lot of cultural items has been requested for repatriation. The one lot of unassociated funerary objects are one lot of worked faunal bone. On an unknown date, an unknown collector collected the cultural materials from mounds on an unknown site in the Sacramento Valley, CA. Mrs. Thomas E. Fleming Jr. donated the cultural materials to the Southwest Museum in 1940.
A total of two lots of cultural items has been requested for repatriation. The two lots of unassociated funerary objects are one baked clay object and one lot of worked shell. On an unknown date, archaeologist Franklin R. Johnston collected the cultural materials from unknown sites in the Sacramento Valley, CA. Mr. Johnston donated the cultural materials to the Southwest Museum in 1944.
A total of one lot of cultural items has been requested for repatriation. The one lot of unassociated funerary objects are one lot of worked shell. On an unknown date, Mr. Harry Brisley collected the cultural material from an unknown site in the Sacramento Valley, CA. Mr. Brisley donated the cultural materials to the Southwest Museum in 1947.
A total of one cultural item has been requested for repatriation. The one unassociated funerary object is one sandstone ground stone. On an unknown date, Max Fisher collected the mortar fragments from an unknown site in the Sacramento Valley, CA. Mrs. Bertha H. Heise donated the cultural material to the Southwest Museum in 1948.
A total of one lot of cultural items has been requested for repatriation. The one lot of unassociated funerary objects are one lot of ornaments. On an unknown date, Mrs. Gladys Knight Harris collected the cultural material from an unknown site in the Sacramento Valley, CA.. Harris's son, Mr. Knight Harris, donated the cultural materials to the Southwest Museum, now a part of the Autry Museum, in 1983.
Determinations
The Autry Museum of the American West has determined that:
The 99 lots of unassociated funerary objects described in this notice are reasonably believed to have been placed intentionally with or near human remains, and are connected, either at the time of death or later as part of the death rite or ceremony of a Native American culture according to the Native American traditional knowledge of a lineal descendant, Indian Tribe, or Native Hawaiian organization. The unassociated funerary objects have been identified by a preponderance of the evidence as related to human remains, specific individuals, or families, or removed from a specific burial site or burial area of an individual or individuals with cultural affiliation to an Indian Tribe or Native Hawaiian organization.
The one object of cultural patrimony described in this notice have ongoing historical, traditional, or cultural importance central to the Native American group, including any constituent sub-group (such as a band, clan, lineage, ceremonial society, or other subdivision), according to the Native American traditional knowledge of an Indian Tribe or Native Hawaiian organization.
There is a connection between the cultural items described in this notice and the Ione Band of Miwok Indians of California; Shingle Springs Band of Miwok Indians, Shingle Springs Rancheria (Verona Tract), California; United Auburn Indian Community of the Auburn Rancheria of California; and the Wilton Rancheria, California.
Requests for Repatriation
Additional, written requests for repatriation of the cultural items in this notice must be sent to the authorized representative identified in this notice under
ADDRESSES
. Requests for repatriation may be submitted by any lineal descendant, Indian Tribe, or Native Hawaiian organization not identified in this notice who shows, by a preponderance of the evidence, that the requestor is a lineal descendant or
(

a culturally affiliated Indian Tribe or Native Hawaiian organization.
Repatriation of the cultural items in this notice to a requestor may occur on or after November 23, 2026. If competing requests for repatriation are received, the Autry Museum of the American West must determine the most appropriate requestor prior to repatriation. Requests for joint repatriation of the cultural items are considered a single request and not competing requests. The Autry Museum of the American West is responsible for sending a copy of this notice to the Indian Tribes and Native Hawaiian organizations identified in this notice and to any other consulting parties.

ACTION:
Notice.
SUMMARY:
In accordance with the Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act (NAGPRA), the Office
(
printed page 66729)
of the State Archaeologist Bioarchaeology Program (OSA BP) has completed an inventory of human remains and has determined that there is a cultural affiliation between the human remains and Indian Tribes or Native Hawaiian organizations in this notice.
DATES:
Repatriation of the human remains in this notice may occur on or after November 23, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
Send written requests for repatriation of the human remains in this notice to Dr. Lara Noldner, Office of the State Archaeologist Bioarchaeology Program, University of Iowa, 700 S Clinton Street, Iowa City, IA 52242, email
lara-noldner@uiowa.edu
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
This notice is published as part of the National Park Service's administrative responsibilities under NAGPRA. The determinations in this notice are the sole responsibility of the OSA BP, and additional information on the determinations in this notice, including the results of consultation, can be found in its inventory or related records. The National Park Service is not responsible for the determinations in this notice.
Abstract of Information Available
Human remains representing, at least, one individual have been identified. No associated funerary objects are present. These human remains were collected by a private citizen in the Loess Hills near Pisgah, IA in the 1930s. They were found in the estate of decedent Arthur Henderson in July 2026 and transferred to the State Medical Examiner's Office (IOSME#26-06865) where they were determined to be ancient and not of medico-legal significance. The human remains were then transferred to the OSA in late August 2026. One adult male of Native American ancestry is represented (BP4083). No hazardous substances were used to treat the human remains.
Cultural Affiliation
Based on the information available and the results of consultation, cultural affiliation is reasonably identified by the geographical location or acquisition history of the human remains described in this notice.
Determinations
The OSA BP has determined that:
The human remains described in this notice represent the physical remains of one individual of Native American ancestry.
There is a connection between the human remains described in this notice and the Cheyenne River Sioux Tribe of the Cheyenne River Reservation, South Dakota; Citizen Potawatomi Nation, Oklahoma; Flandreau Santee Sioux Tribe of South Dakota; Ho-Chunk Nation of Wisconsin; Iowa Tribe of Kansas and Nebraska; Iowa Tribe of Oklahoma; Lower Sioux Indian Community in the State of Minnesota; Miami Tribe of Oklahoma; Omaha Tribe of Nebraska; Otoe-Missouria Tribe of Indians, Oklahoma; Pawnee Nation of Oklahoma; Peoria Tribe of Indians of Oklahoma; Ponca Tribe of Indians of Oklahoma; Ponca Tribe of Nebraska; Prairie Band Potawatomi Nation; Prairie Island Indian Community in the State of Minnesota; Sac & Fox Nation of Missouri in Kansas and Nebraska; Sac & Fox Nation, Oklahoma; Sac & Fox Tribe of the Mississippi in Iowa; Santee Sioux Nation, Nebraska; Sisseton-Wahpeton Oyate of the Lake Traverse Reservation, South Dakota; Spirit Lake Tribe, North Dakota; The Osage Nation; Three Affiliated Tribes of the Fort Berthold Reservation, North Dakota; Upper Sioux Community, Minnesota; Winnebago Tribe of Nebraska; and the Yankton Sioux Tribe of South Dakota.
Requests for Repatriation
Written requests for repatriation of the human remains in this notice must be sent to the authorized representative identified in this notice under
ADDRESSES
. Requests for repatriation may be submitted by:
1. Any one or more of the Indian Tribes or Native Hawaiian organizations identified in this notice.
2. Any lineal descendant, Indian Tribe, or Native Hawaiian organization not identified in this notice who shows, by a preponderance of the evidence, that the requestor is a lineal descendant or an Indian Tribe or Native Hawaiian organization with cultural affiliation.
Repatriation of the human remains described in this notice to a requestor may occur on or after November 23, 2026. If competing requests for repatriation are received, the OSA BP must determine the most appropriate requestor prior to repatriation. Requests for joint repatriation of the human remains are considered a single request and not competing requests. The OSA BP is responsible for sending a copy of this notice to the Indian Tribes and Native Hawaiian organizations identified in this notice and any other consulting parties.

Metal Container (MCC) LP submitted a notification of proposed production activity to the FTZ Board (the Board) for its facility in Jacksonville, Florida within FTZ 64. The notification conforming to the requirements of the Board's regulations (

) was received on September 30, 2026.

15 CFR 400.14(b)
, FTZ production activity would be limited to the specific foreign-status material/component and specific finished product described in the submitted notification (summarized below) and subsequently authorized by the Board. 19 CFR 146.41
).

ftz@trade.gov
.
The closing period for their receipt is December 1, 2026.
A copy of the notification will be available for public inspection in the “Online FTZ Information System” section of the Board's website.

ACTION:
Notice.
SUMMARY:
In accordance with the Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act (NAGPRA), Sonoma State University has completed an inventory of human remains and associated funerary objects and has determined that there is a cultural affiliation between the human remains and associated funerary objects and Indian Tribes or Native Hawaiian organizations in this notice.
DATES:
Repatriation of the human remains and associated funerary objects in this notice may occur on or after November 23, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
Send written requests for repatriation of the human remains and associated funerary objects in this notice to Kirsten Twork, Sonoma State University, 1801 E Cotati Avenue, Rohnert Park, CA 94928, email
tworkk@sonoma.edu
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
This notice is published as part of the National Park Service's administrative responsibilities under NAGPRA. The determinations in this notice are the sole responsibility of the Sonoma State University, and additional information on the determinations in this notice, including the results of consultation, can be found in its inventory or related records. The National Park Service is not responsible for the determinations in this notice.
Abstract of Information Available
Human remains representing at least two individuals were requested for repatriation. The 717 lots of associated funerary objects are unmodified shell, unmodified flakes, modified flakes, historic material, unmodified faunal bone, and cobble stone tools. The individuals and associated funerary objects were removed from CA-SON-321 originating in Bodega Bay, California. The Ancestors and material was removed from the site due to a planned project to expand housing of the Bodega Bay Marine Lab. The material has been housed at SSU since 1989.
The 71 lots of associated funerary objects are flaked stone debitage, unmodified shell, and historic material. The associated funerary objects were removed from CA-SON-1526, CA-SON-1527, CA-SON-1528, CA-SON-1529, CA-SON-1530, and CA-SON-1531/H in Santa Rosa, in Sonoma County, California. At the time of their removal no burials were identified. However, during an unrelated excavation at a later date burials were identified at CA-SON-1530. The material housed as Sonoma State University was removed from its location during an archaeological survey for a proposed sewerage system master plan for the South Wright Road Area. Since 1986 the cultural material has resided at Sonoma State University.
The 21 lots of associated funerary objects are flaked stone debitage and modified flaked stone tools. The associated funerary objects were removed from CA-SON-1776/H originating in Eldridge, California. The material was removed from the site during an archaeological review of the site at the request of the property owners in accordance with Sonoma County Department of Planning regarding adjustments to property lines. The material has been housed at SSU since 1989.
The 144 lots of associated funerary objects are flaked stone debitage, flaked stone tools, quartz crystals, groundstone tools, and unmodified faunal bone. The associated funerary objects were removed from CA-SON-1216 and CA-SON-1217 originating in El Verano, California. The material was removed from the sites during an archaeological review of the George Ranch. The material has been housed at SSU since 1982
The 732 lots of associated funerary objects were removed from CA-SON-298/H in Bodega Bay, California in Sonoma County. The cultural material was removed during an archaeological investigation to determine the impact to the site that may occur during the installation of the proposed sewerage facilities on the Bodega Bay Public Utility District. The items include groundstone tools, modified stone tools,
(
printed page 66731)
flaked stone debitage, flotation samples, unmodified faunal, organic material, unmodified shell, modified shell, clay, quartz, and historics. The cultural items have been at Sonoma State University since 1985.
The 758 lots of associated funerary objects were removed from CA-SON-40 in Kenwood, California in Sonoma County. The cultural material was removed during three different instances during the 1980s to 1990, all related to the construction of a winery. The items include groundstone tools, modified stone tools, flaked stone debitage, soil, unmodified faunal, modified faunal bone, organic material, unmodified shell, modified shell, quartz, and historics. The cultural items have been at Sonoma State University since they were removed from their location.
The 13 lots of associated funerary objects were removed from CA-SON-113 in Glen Ellen, California in Sonoma County. The cultural material was removed during two different instances in 1978 and 2009. The portion of the material from 1978 was removed related to an archaeological survey for the Glen Ellen Wastewater Collection System and the 2009 portion was donated to the university by the land owner. The items include groundstone tools, modified stone tools, flaked stone debitage, and historics. The cultural items have been at Sonoma State University since they were brought to the university.
The three lots of associated funerary objects were removed from CA-SON-24 in Santa Rosa, California in Sonoma County. The cultural material was removed during an archaeological survey of the Northern Sonoma Valley. The items include modified stone tools. The cultural items have been at Sonoma State University since 1984.
Human remains representing at least one individual were requested for repatriation. The 23 lots of associated funerary objects are unmodified shell, unmodified flakes, modified flakes, historic material, unmodified faunal bone, organics, and soil. The Ancestor and associated funerary objects were removed from CA-SON-326 originating in Bodega Bay, California. Information related to why the ancestor and material was removed from the site was not located. The material has been housed at SSU since 1974.
The one lot of associated funerary objects were removed from CA-SON-302 in Bodega Bay, California in Sonoma County. Information related to why the material was removed from the site was not located.The items include modified stone tools. The cultural items have been at Sonoma State University since 1976.
The six lots of associated funerary objects were removed from CA-SON-306 in Bodega Bay, California in Sonoma County. The cultural material was removed during an archaeological survey related to housing development. The items include flaked stone debitage and quartz crystal. The cultural items have been at Sonoma State University since 1982.
The one lot of associated funerary objects are modified stone tools. The associated funerary objects were removed from CA-SON-338 originating in Salmon Creek, California. No information as to why the item was removed from the site was located at this time. The material has been housed at SSU since 1993.
The 110 lots of associated funerary objects include debitage, modified stone tools, modified shell, unmodified shell, and unmodified faunal bone. The cultural materials were removed from CA-SON-659 in Sereno del Mar, California in Sonoma county. The material was removed from the sites during an archaeological survey. The cultural material has been housed at SSU since 1975.
In the case of missing cultural items, all items when located will also be repatriated from the collections discussed above. Based on records concerning the ancestors and cultural items and the institution in which they are housed, there is no evidence of the items being treated with hazardous substances.
Cultural Affiliation
Based on the information available and the results of consultation, cultural affiliation is reasonably identified by the geographical location or acquisition history of the human remains and associated funerary objects described in this notice.
Determinations
Sonoma State University has determined that:
The human remains described in this notice represent the physical remains of three individuals of Native American ancestry.
The 2,600 lots of objects described in this notice are reasonably believed to have been placed intentionally with or near individual human remains at the time of death or later as part of the death rite or ceremony.
There is a connection between the human remains and associated funerary objects described in this notice and the Federated Indians of Graton Rancheria, California.
Requests for Repatriation
Written requests for repatriation of the human remains and associated funerary objects in this notice must be sent to the authorized representative identified in this notice under
ADDRESSES
. Requests for repatriation may be submitted by:
1. Any one or more of the Indian Tribes or Native Hawaiian organizations identified in this notice.
2. Any lineal descendant, Indian Tribe, or Native Hawaiian organization not identified in this notice who shows, by a preponderance of the evidence, that the requestor is a lineal descendant or an Indian Tribe or Native Hawaiian organization with cultural affiliation.
Repatriation of the human remains and associated funerary objects described in this notice to a requestor may occur on or after November 23, 2026. If competing requests for repatriation are received, Sonoma State University must determine the most appropriate requestor prior to repatriation. Requests for joint repatriation of the human remains and associated funerary objects are considered a single request and not competing requests. Sonoma State University is responsible for sending a copy of this notice to the Indian Tribes and Native Hawaiian organizations identified in this notice and any other consulting parties.

, and the implementing regulations,

.

SUMMARY:
In accordance with the Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act (NAGPRA), the U.S. Department of the Interior, Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA), has completed an inventory of human remains and has determined that there is a cultural affiliation between the human remains and Indian Tribes or Native Hawaiian organizations in this notice.
DATES:
Repatriation of the human remains in this notice may occur on or after November 23, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
Send written requests for repatriation of the human remains in this notice to Tamara Billie, U.S. Department of Interior, Bureau of Indian Affairs, 1001 Indian School Road NW, Mailbox 44, Albuquerque, NM 87104, email
tamara.billie@bia.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
This notice is published as part of the National Park Service's administrative responsibilities under NAGPRA. The determinations in this notice are the sole responsibility of the BIA, and additional information on the determinations in this notice, including the results of consultation, can be found in its inventory or related records. The National Park Service is not responsible for the determinations in this notice.
Abstract of Information Available
Human remains representing at least, one individual has been identified. No associated funerary objects are present. In 2024, the U.S. Department of the Interior, Bureau of Indian Affairs, was contacted by an individual in California who discovered an Ancestral skull, including cranium and mandible, among her father-in-law's belongings following his passing in 2021. The individual shared a family oral history indicating that the Ancestral skull had been removed by her father-in-law from the Fort Randall Dam area in Gregory
(
printed page 66730)
County and Charles Mix County, South Dakota, during his work on the dam's construction between 1945 and 1947. The individual expressed a desire to repatriate the Ancestral skull and requested that the BIA take the lead in facilitating this process. In March 2025, the BIA subsequently coordinated with the NAGPRA team at the UCLA Fowler Museum to temporarily house the Ancestral skull on a short-term loan, enabling the Bureau to initiate consultation with the Tribal Historic Preservation Officer of the Yankton Sioux Tribe of South Dakota regarding repatriation. At this time, it is unknown whether any potentially hazardous substances were used to treat the Ancestral remains.
Cultural Affiliation
Based on the information available and the results of consultation, cultural affiliation is reasonably identified by the geographical location or acquisition history of the human remains described in this notice.
Determinations
The BIA has determined that:
The human remains described in this notice represent the physical remains of one individual of Native American ancestry.
There is a connection between the human remains described in this notice and the Yankton Sioux Tribe of South Dakota.
Requests for Repatriation

ADDRESSES
. Requests for repatriation may be submitted by:
1. Any one or more of the Indian Tribes or Native Hawaiian organizations identified in this notice.
2. Any lineal descendant, Indian Tribe, or Native Hawaiian organization not identified in this notice who shows, by a preponderance of the evidence, that the requestor is a lineal descendant or an Indian Tribe or Native Hawaiian organization with cultural affiliation.
Repatriation of the human remains described in this notice to a requestor may occur on or after November 23, 2026. If competing requests for repatriation are received, the BIA must determine the most appropriate requestor prior to repatriation. Requests for joint repatriation of the human remains are considered a single request and not competing requests. The BIA is responsible for sending a copy of this notice to the Indian Tribes and Native Hawaiian organizations identified in this notice and any other consulting parties.

The four sacred objects described in this notice are specific ceremonial objects needed by a traditional Native American religious leader for present-day adherents to practice traditional Native American religion, according to the Native American traditional knowledge of a lineal descendant.
Allan Dowsett is connected to the cultural items described in this notice.

AGENCY:
National Park Service, Interior.
ACTION:
Notice.
SUMMARY:
In accordance with the Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act (NAGPRA), Sonoma State University intends to repatriate certain cultural items that meet the definition of unassociated funerary objects, sacred objects, and/or objects of cultural patrimony and that have a cultural affiliation with the Indian Tribes or Native Hawaiian organizations in this notice.
DATES:
Repatriation of the cultural items in this notice may occur on or after November 23, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
Send additional, written requests for repatriation of the cultural items in this notice to Kirsten Twork, Sonoma State University, 1801 E Cotati Avenue, Rohnert Park, CA 94928, email
tworkk@sonoma.edu
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
This notice is published as part of the National Park Service's administrative responsibilities under NAGPRA. The determinations in this notice are the sole responsibility of Sonoma State University, and additional information on the determinations in this notice, including the results of consultation, can be found in the summary or related records. The National Park Service is not responsible for the determinations in this notice.
Abstract of Information Available
A total of 48,638 lots of cultural items have been requested for repatriation. Of the cultural items being requested, 22,648 lots are unassociated funerary objects and 25,990 lots are objects of cultural patrimony.
The 1,789 lots of objects of cultural patrimony were removed from CA-SON-1200 in Santa Rosa, California in Sonoma County. The cultural material was removed from the site during an archaeological investigation at the request of the Pacific Gas & Electric Company. The items include modified stone tools, debitage, soil, stone beads, groundstone, historics, unmodified faunal bone. The cultural items have been at Sonoma State University (SSU) since 1980.
The 549 lots of unassociated funerary objects were removed from CA-SON-920 in Santa Rosa, California in Sonoma County. The cultural material was removed during two instances, in 1976 and 1977. In 1976 Sonoma State University conducted a field survey related to housing and business development. The material from 1977 is related to an additional field survey and test excavation of the site. The items include modified stone, unmodified faunal, modified shell, modified faunal, debitage, and historics. The cultural items have been at SSU since its removal.
The 1,522 lots of unassociated funerary objects were removed from CA-SON-963 and CA-SON-964 in Santa Rosa, California in Sonoma County. The cultural material was removed related to a residential development plan by Trivest Development Company. The items include petrified wood sticks, groundstone tools, flaked stone debitage, flaked stone tools, historic material, unmodified faunal, organic material, stone material, and soil. The cultural items have been at SSU since 1984.
The 10,792 lots of unassociated funerary objects were removed from CA-SON-1269 in Santa Rosa, California in Sonoma County. The cultural material was removed during an archaeological investigation at the request of the Sonoma County Planning Department. The items include groundstone tools, modified stone tools, flaked stone debitage, soil, gravel, float samples, modified faunal, unmodified faunal, organic material, unmodified shell, modified shell, clay, fire affected rock, petrified wood, organics, and historic material. The cultural items have been at SSU since 1981.

The items include flaked stone debitage, flaked stone tools, groundstone tools, and historic material. The cultural material has been housed at SSU since its removal.
The 668 lots of unassociated funerary objects were removed during archaeological surveys in Windsor, California in Sonoma County. The ASC surveyed sites CA-SON-1120, CA-SON-1212, CA-SON-1322, and CA-SON-1388 due to land development between 1970 and 1990. The items include flaked stone debitage, flaked stone tools, and groundstone tools. The cultural material has been housed at SSU since its removal.
The 3,087 lots of objects of cultural patrimony were removed during archaeological surveys in the city of Sonoma, California in Sonoma County related to land development. The surveys were conducted by the ASC from 1970 to 2000. Sites surveyed include CA-SON-1238, CA-SON-1323, CA-SON-1324, the Windsor Trailer Camp, and Yerba Buena Subdivision. The items include flaked stone debitage, flaked stone tools, petrified wood, groundstone tools, modified faunal bone, baked clay unmodified faunal bone, charmstones, ochre, soil, organic material, and historic material. The cultural material has been housed at SSU since its removal.
The six lots of unassociated funerary objects were removed from CA-SON-1803 in Petaluma, California in Sonoma County. The material was removed during an archaeological investigation for the development of a subdivision. The items include flaked stone debitage. The cultural material has been housed at SSU since 1989.
(
printed page 66713)
The five lots of objects of cultural patrimony were removed from CA-SON-1812 in Petaluma, California in Sonoma County. The material was removed from the sites during an archaeological investigation related to the development of a subdivision. The items include flaked stone debitage. The cultural material has been housed at SSU since 1990.
The one lot of unassociated funerary objects were removed from CA-MRN-9 in Mill Valley, California in Marin County. No information related to the removal of material from the site was located. The items include modified shell. It is unknown when the material came to SSU.
In the case of missing cultural items, any additional items when located will also be repatriated from the collections discussed above. Based on records concerning the cultural items and the institution in which they are housed, there is no evidence of the items being treated with hazardous substances.
Determinations
Sonoma State University has determined that:
The 22,648 lots of unassociated funerary objects described in this notice are reasonably believed to have been placed intentionally with or near human remains, and are connected, either at the time of death or later as part of the death rite or ceremony of a Native American culture according to the Native American traditional knowledge of a lineal descendant, Indian Tribe, or Native Hawaiian organization. The unassociated funerary objects have been identified by a preponderance of the evidence as related to human remains, specific individuals, or families, or removed from a specific burial site or burial area of an individual or individuals with cultural affiliation to an Indian Tribe or Native Hawaiian organization.
The 25,990 lots of objects of cultural patrimony described in this notice are specific ceremonial objects needed by a traditional Native American religious leader for present-day adherents to practice traditional Native American religion, according to the Native American traditional knowledge of a lineal descendant, Indian Tribe, or Native Hawaiian organization.
There is a connection between the cultural items described in this notice and the Federated Indians of Graton Rancheria, California.
Requests for Repatriation
Additional, written requests for repatriation of the cultural items in this notice must be sent to the authorized representative identified in this notice under
ADDRESSES
. Requests for repatriation may be submitted by any lineal descendant, Indian Tribe, or Native Hawaiian organization not identified in this notice who shows, by a preponderance of the evidence, that the requestor is a lineal descendant or a culturally affiliated Indian Tribe or Native Hawaiian organization.
Repatriation of the cultural items in this notice to a requestor may occur on or after November 23, 2026. If competing requests for repatriation are received, Sonoma State University must determine the most appropriate requestor prior to repatriation. Requests for joint repatriation of the cultural items are considered a single request and not competing requests. The Sonoma State University is responsible for sending a copy of this notice to the Indian Tribes and Native Hawaiian organizations identified in this notice and to any other consulting parties.

SUMMARY:
In accordance with the Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act (NAGPRA), California State University, Fullerton (CSUF) intends to repatriate certain cultural items that meet the definition of unassociated funerary objects or objects of cultural patrimony and that have a cultural affiliation with the Indian Tribes or Native Hawaiian organizations in this notice.
DATES:
Repatriation of the cultural items in this notice may occur on or after November 23, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
Send additional, written requests for repatriation of the cultural items in this notice to Sean Walker, California State University, Fullerton, 2600 Nutwood Avenue, Fullerton, CA 92831, email
SWALKER@FULLERTON.EDU
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
This notice is published as part of the National Park Service's administrative responsibilities under NAGPRA. The determinations in this notice are the sole responsibility of CSUF, and additional information on the determinations in this notice, including the results of consultation, can be found in the summary or related records. The National Park Service is not responsible for the determinations in this notice.
Abstract of Information Available
A total of 979 cultural items have been requested for repatriation. The 232 unassociated funerary objects are ceramic vessels and sherds, beads, manos and mano fragments, chipped stone tools, debitage, hammerstones, mauls, projectile points, and shell. The 747 objects of cultural patrimony include ceramic vessels and sherds, beads, manos, metates, a pestle, debitage, shell, modified faunal bone including bone awls, chipped stone tools, abraders, a shaft straightener, hammerstones, mauls, modified stone, a stone mortar, faunal bone, pendants, organic material, projectile points, and one lot of uncategorized cultural material.
Unassociated funerary objects and objects of cultural patrimony were collected by Earl and Mildred Wilson, private collectors that focused primarily on areas of New Mexico and Arizona in the 1950s and 1960s. The Wilsons numbered their collecting locations from 0 to 53 and recorded them on hand-drawn maps and with annotations on an Arizona/New Mexico road map. Notebooks from the Wilsons contain detailed descriptions of objects, locations, and dates of collection. Unnumbered but named collecting locations include Pete Bacca's Ranch, Candelaria Ranch, Bibo's Ranch, Floyd Lee Ranch, Grants, NM, in the sand hills, Mirabel's Ranch, and near Milan, NM. The Wilsons wrote that most cultural items were removed from locations in the vicinity of Grants, NM and most were from areas along NM State Road 117. Wilson locations #21, 27, 35, and 46 were noted as sites of human burials. The cultural items were brought to CSUF in 1974 for curation. The university purchased the collection in 1981 and recorded it as Accession #1.
Additional objects of cultural patrimony consisting of a basaltic lava stone mortar and metate were also identified. These items (Acc. 95.24, Acc. 95.25) were donated to CSUF by Charles Ruby, a private collector, in 1983.
CSUF has not identified any records indicating the presence of any potentially hazardous substances used to treat any of the cultural items.
Determinations
CSUF has determined that:
The 232 unassociated funerary objects described in this notice are reasonably believed to have been placed intentionally with or near human remains, and are connected, either at the time of death or later as part of the death rite or ceremony of a Native American culture according to the Native American traditional knowledge of a lineal descendant, Indian Tribe, or Native Hawaiian organization. The unassociated funerary objects have been identified by a preponderance of the evidence as related to human remains, specific individuals, or families, or removed from a specific burial site or burial area of an individual or individuals with cultural affiliation to an Indian Tribe or Native Hawaiian organization.
The 747 objects of cultural patrimony described in this notice have ongoing historical, traditional, or cultural importance central to the Native American group, including any constituent sub-group (such as a band, clan, lineage, ceremonial society, or other subdivision), according to the Native American traditional knowledge of an Indian Tribe or Native Hawaiian organization.
There is a connection between the cultural items described in this notice and the Pueblo of Acoma, New Mexico.

Additional, written requests for repatriation of the cultural items in this notice must be sent to the authorized representative identified in this notice under
ADDRESSES
. Requests for repatriation may be submitted by any lineal descendant, Indian Tribe, or Native Hawaiian organization not identified in this notice who shows, by a preponderance of the evidence, that the requestor is a lineal descendant or a culturally affiliated Indian Tribe or Native Hawaiian organization.
Repatriation of the cultural items in this notice to a requestor may occur on or after November 23, 2026. If competing requests for repatriation are received, CSUF must determine the most appropriate requestor prior to repatriation. Requests for joint repatriation of the cultural items are considered a single request and not competing requests. CSUF is responsible for sending a copy of this notice to the Indian Tribes and Native Hawaiian organizations identified in this notice and to any other consulting parties.

.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
This notice is published as part of the National Park Service's administrative responsibilities under NAGPRA. Abstract of Information Available
A total of 146 unassociated funerary objects removed from locations in New Mexico have been requested for repatriation.
Of the 146 unassociated funerary objects, a total of one is a lot of copper concretions that was removed from an unknown provenience in the San Juan Watershed by Theophil Mitchell Prudden, Yale University graduate, sometime between 1873 and 1906. The collection was received at the Yale Peabody Museum on April 21, 1906.
Of the 146 unassociated funerary objects, a total of two are ceramic items that were removed from Chaco Canyon in 1896 by Theophil Mitchell Prudden, Yale University graduate. The items are one jar and one lot of bowls. The collection was received at the Yale Peabody Museum on April 21, 1906.
Of the 146 unassociated funerary objects, a total of 71 are ceramic items that were removed from the C-F ranch site in the Mangas Valley in Grant County in 1938 by John Rodman Paul, professor at the Yale School of Medicine. The items are three black-on-white bowls, 61 sherds, 6 lots of sherds, and one lug handle. An exact location for this provenience is not known. The collection was received at the Yale Peabody Museum in January 1940.
Of the 146 unassociated funerary objects, a total of 68 are ceramic, stone, and bone items that were removed from the Thompson Ruin in the Mangas Valley in Grant County in 1938 by John Rodman Paul, professor at the Yale School of Medicine. The ceramic items are one Classic Mimbres black-on-white bowl, 48 sherds, 13 lots of sherds, one olla fragment, and one lug. The stone items are one stone and one lot of stone. The bone items are two faunal bone fragments. An exact location for this provenience is not known. The collection was received at the Yale Peabody Museum in January 1940.
Of the 146 unassociated funerary objects, a total of one is a Mimbres Classic black-on-white bowl that was removed from an unknown provenience in the Southwest and purchased by the Yale Peabody Museum from Earl Gilmore; the item was removed by Gilmore's brother. The collection was received at the Yale Peabody Museum on June 11, 1974.
Of the 146 unassociated funerary objects, a total of one is a black-on-white bowl that was removed from an unknown provenience in the Southwest and donated to the Yale Peabody Museum by Anni Albers. The collection was received at the Yale Peabody Museum on December 20, 1979.
Of the 146 unassociated funerary objects, a total of one is a game ball removed from a Mimbres grave on ranchland in an unknown location in New Mexico by an unknown collector and donated to the Yale Peabody Museum by Peter David Joralemon. The collection was received at the Yale Peabody Museum on December 20, 1984.
Of the 146 unassociated funerary objects, a total of one is a Mimbres black-on-white bowl that was removed from an unknown provenience in New Mexico. The bowl was originally part of the collection of Peter G. Wray and was donated to the Yale Peabody Museum by Peter David Joralemon. The collection was received at the Yale Peabody Museum on December 30, 1991.
Determinations
The Yale Peabody Museum has determined that:
The 146 unassociated funerary objects described in this notice are reasonably believed to have been placed intentionally with or near human remains, and are connected, either at the time of death or later as part of the death rite or ceremony of a Native American culture according to the Native American traditional knowledge of a lineal descendant, Indian Tribe, or Native Hawaiian organization. The unassociated funerary objects have been identified by a preponderance of the evidence as related to human remains, specific individuals, or families, or removed from a specific burial site or burial area of an individual or individuals with cultural affiliation to an Indian Tribe or Native Hawaiian organization.
There is a connection between the cultural items described in this notice and the Hopi Tribe of Arizona; Navajo Nation, Arizona, New Mexico, & Utah; Ohkay Owingeh, New Mexico; Pueblo of Acoma, New Mexico; Pueblo of Cochiti, New Mexico; Pueblo of Isleta, New Mexico; Pueblo of Jemez, New Mexico; Pueblo of Laguna, New Mexico; Pueblo of Nambe, New Mexico; Pueblo of Picuris, New Mexico; Pueblo of Pojoaque, New Mexico; Pueblo of San Felipe, New Mexico; Pueblo of San Ildefonso, New Mexico; Pueblo of Sandia, New Mexico; Pueblo of Santa Ana, New Mexico; Pueblo of Santa Clara, New Mexico; Pueblo of Taos, New Mexico; Pueblo of Tesuque, New Mexico; Pueblo of Zia, New Mexico; Santo Domingo Pueblo; Ysleta del Sur Pueblo; and the Zuni Tribe of the Zuni Reservation, New Mexico.

. Requests for repatriation may be submitted by any lineal descendant, Indian Tribe, or Native Hawaiian organization not identified in this notice who shows, by a preponderance of the evidence, that the requestor is a lineal descendant or a culturally affiliated Indian Tribe or Native Hawaiian organization.
Repatriation of the cultural items in this notice to a requestor may occur on or after November 23, 2026. In accordance with the Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act (NAGPRA), Indiana University has completed an inventory of human remains and associated funerary objects and has determined that there is a cultural affiliation between the human remains and Indian Tribes or Native Hawaiian organizations in this notice.
DATES:
Repatriation of the human remains and associated funerary objects in this notice may occur on or after November 23, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
Send written requests for repatriation of the human remains and associated funerary objects in this notice to Dr. Jayne-Leigh Thomas, Office of the Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act (NAGPRA), Indiana University, Student Building 318, 701 E Kirkwood Avenue, Bloomington, IN 47405, email
thomajay@iu.edu
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
This notice is published as part of the National Park Service's administrative responsibilities under NAGPRA. Abstract of Information Available
Human remains representing, at least, one individual have been identified. The two associated funerary objects are one lot of copper and one lot of sand. This collection was excavated from 12Fu3 during construction of S.R. 10 in Fulton County, Indiana in 1954. There is no known presence of any potentially hazardous substances.
Human remains, representing, at least, one individual have been identified. There are no known associated funerary objects. This collection was excavated from an unknown location in Lake County, Indiana on an unknown date. There is no known presence of any potentially hazardous substances.
Human remains, representing, at least, one individual have been identified. The six associated funerary objects are one lot of lithics, one lot of faunal bones, one lot of worked bone, one lot of shell, one lot of worked shell, and one lot of ceramic/clay artifacts. This collection was excavated from the Griesmer Site in Lake County, Indiana in 1962 as part of an Indiana University field school.
Human remains, representing, at least, one individual have been identified. There are no associated funerary objects. This collection was discovered by Mr. Charles Faulkner on an unknown date from the Lake County site (12La166). It was donated to IU by Mr. Oha Zamazel in 1960. There is no known presence of any potentially hazardous substances.
Human remains, representing, at least, one individual have been identified. There are no associated funerary objects. This collection was discovered in 1933 by WPA workers three miles south of Plymouth in Marshall County, Indiana. There is no known presence of any potentially hazardous substances.
Human remains, representing, at least one individual have been identified. The one associated funerary object is one lot of historic artifacts. This collection was discovered in 1950 from an unnamed site (12Mr232) in Marshall County by Mr. Charles Faulkner. It was donated to Indiana University in 1960 by Mr. Al Runnels. There is no known presence of any potentially hazardous substances.
The two associated funerary objects are one lot of lithics and one lot of soil. The artifacts were collection in 1932 from Vergin Mound (12Pr28), Porter County, by Mr. J. Gilbert McAllister. There is no known presence of any potentially hazardous substances.
Human remains, representing, at least seven individuals have been identified. The eight associated funerary objects are one lot of clay/ceramics objects, one lot of lithics, one lot of charcoal, one lot of soil, one lot of plant materials, one lot of copper, one lot of shell, and one lot of mixed materials. This collection was excavated from Weise Mound (12Pr35) in Porter County, Indiana. There is no known presence of any potentially hazardous substances.
Human remains, representing, at least two individuals have been identified. The five associated funerary objects are one lot of faunal bones, one lot of worked bone, one lot of historic artifacts, one lot of clay/ceramics, and one lot of shell. This collection was excavated from the Fifield site (12Pr55) in Porter County, Indiana. There is no known presence of any potentially hazardous substances.
Human remains, representing, at least, 37 individuals have been identified. The seven associated funerary objects are one lot of faunal bones, one lot of stone, one lot of worked stone, one lot of lithics, one lot of red ochre, one lot of copper, and one lot of shell. This collection was discovered at the Butterfield Camp site (12Wh2) in White County, Indiana by Mr. Jack Householder in 1952. There is no known presence of any potentially hazardous substances.
Cultural Affiliation
Based on the information available and the results of consultation, cultural affiliation is clearly identified by the information available about the human remains and associated funerary objects described in this notice.
Determinations
Indiana University has determined that:
The human remains described in this notice represent the physical
(
printed page 66736)
remains of 52 individuals of Native American ancestry.
The 31 objects described in this notice is reasonably believed to have been placed intentionally with or near individual human remains at the time of death or later as part of the death rite or ceremony.
There is a connection between the human remains and associated funerary objects described in this notice and the Absentee-Shawnee Tribe of Indians of Oklahoma; Citizen Potawatomi Nation, Oklahoma; Forest County Potawatomi Community, Wisconsin; Iowa Tribe of Kansas and Nebraska; Match-E-Be-Nash-She-Wish Band of Pottawatomi (previously listed as Match-E-Be-Nash-She-Wish Band of Pottawatomi Indians of Michigan); Miami Tribe of Oklahoma; Minnesota Chippewa Tribe, Minnesota (Mille Lacs Band); Nottawaseppi Huron Band of the Potawatomi, Michigan; Peoria Tribe of Indians of Oklahoma; Pokagon Band of Potawatomi Indians, Michigan and Indiana; Ponca Tribe of Nebraska; and the Sac & Fox Tribe of the Mississippi in Iowa.
Requests for Repatriation
Written requests for repatriation of the human remains and associated funerary objects in this notice must be sent to the authorized representative identified in this notice under
ADDRESSES
. Requests for repatriation may be submitted by:
1. Any one or more of the Indian Tribes or Native Hawaiian organizations identified in this notice.
2. Any lineal descendant, Indian Tribe, or Native Hawaiian organization not identified in this notice who shows, by a preponderance of the evidence, that the requestor is a lineal descendant or an Indian Tribe or Native Hawaiian organization with cultural affiliation.
Repatriation of the human remains and associated funerary objects described in this notice to a requestor may occur on or after November 23, 2026. If competing requests for repatriation are received, Indiana University must determine the most appropriate requestor prior to repatriation. Requests for joint repatriation of the human remains and associated funerary objects are considered a single request and not competing requests. Indiana University is responsible for sending a copy of this notice to the Indian Tribes and Native Hawaiian organizations identified in this notice and any other consulting parties.

Metal Container (MCC) LP submitted a notification of proposed production activity to the FTZ Board (the Board) for its facility in New Windsor, New York within FTZ 37. The notification conforming to the requirements of the Board's regulations (
15 CFR 400.22
) was received on September 30, 2026.

15 CFR 400.14(b)

.

).

. The closing period for their receipt is December 1, 2026.

Chandler.

In accordance with the Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act (NAGPRA), the Field Museum intends to repatriate certain cultural items that meet the definition of unassociated funerary objects, sacred objects, and/or objects of cultural patrimony and that have a cultural affiliation with the Indian Tribes or Native Hawaiian organizations in this notice.
DATES:
Repatriation of the cultural items in this notice may occur on or after November 23, 2026.
ADDRESSES:

.

This notice is published as part of the National Park Service's administrative responsibilities under NAGPRA. The National Park Service is not responsible for the determinations in this notice.
Abstract of Information Available
A total of 96 cultural items have been requested for repatriation. The four unassociated funerary objects are a bowl, a knapper, a chisel, and a basket. The eight sacred objects are four mortars and pestles, two bowls, one medicine, and one feather headband. The 84 objects of cultural patrimony are 47 baskets, 16 basket caps, eight lots of basket materials, three water containers, two meal brushes, two arrow planes, one bow and arrows, one mortar and pestle, one knapper set, one cradle frame, one ball, and one tray. All of the cultural items were removed from various sites in Kern County, California. In 1894, Edward E. Ayer donated three of the baskets to the Field Museum. In 1901, 1902, and 1904, on behalf of the Field Museum, Dr. John Hudson collected 66 of the cultural items on expeditions among the Native populations of California. The Museum accessioned those items during the same years they were collected. In 1920, 1921, 1929, and 1937, Homer E. Sargent donated 27 of the cultural items from his personal collection to the Museum.
Determinations
The Field Museum has determined that:
The four unassociated funerary objects described in this notice are reasonably believed to have been placed intentionally with or near human remains, and is connected, either at the time of death or later as part of the death rite or ceremony of a Native American culture according to the Native American traditional knowledge of a lineal descendant, Indian Tribe, or Native Hawaiian organization. The unassociated funerary objects have been identified by a preponderance of the evidence as related to human remains, specific individuals, or families, or removed from a specific burial site or burial area of an individual or individuals with cultural affiliation to an Indian Tribe or Native Hawaiian organization.
The eight sacred objects described in this notice are specific ceremonial objects needed by a traditional Native American religious leader for present-day adherents to practice traditional Native American religion, according to the Native American traditional knowledge of a lineal descendant, Indian Tribe, or Native Hawaiian organization.
The 84 objects of cultural patrimony described in this notice have ongoing historical, traditional, or cultural importance central to the Native American group, including any constituent sub-group (such as a band, clan, lineage, ceremonial society, or other subdivision), according to the Native American traditional knowledge of an Indian Tribe or Native Hawaiian organization.
There is a connection between the cultural items described in this notice and the Tejon Indian Tribe.

, FTZ production activity would be limited to the specific foreign-status material/component and specific finished product described in the submitted notification (summarized below) and subsequently authorized by the Board. 19 CFR 146.41
).

DATES:

ADDRESSES:
Send written requests for repatriation of the human remains and associated funerary objects in this notice to Professor David Skelly, Director, Yale Peabody Museum, P.O. Box 208118, New Haven, CT 06520-8118, email
david.skelly@yale.edu
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
This notice is published as part of the National Park Service's administrative responsibilities under NAGPRA. The determinations in this notice are the sole responsibility of the Yale Peabody Museum, and additional information on the determinations in this notice, including the results of consultation, can be found in its inventory or related records. Abstract of Information Available
Human remains representing, at least, five individuals have been identified. No associated funerary objects are present. The collection was removed from a Pueblo burying ground near Abiquiu in Rio Arriba County, in the immediate vicinity of Poshuouinge Pueblo by David Baldwin, Yale University graduate, in 1878. The collection was received at the Yale Peabody Museum over the course of three donations on January 16, 1878, March 21, 1878, and June 5, 1878.
Human remains representing, at least, one individual have been identified. The three associated funerary objects are one lot of fabric burial wrappings, one basketry fragment, and one rabbit stick. The collection was removed from Salmon Ruins, a Chacoan Ancestral Pueblo site in San Juan County, by Christian Snyder on January 1, 1879. David Baldwin assisted Snyder in donating the collection to the Yale Peabody Museum, where it was received on March 29, 1879.
Human remains representing, at least, two individuals have been identified. No associated funerary objects are present. The collection was removed from an unknown location in an unknown county within the San Juan Watershed, by Theophil Mitchell Prudden, Yale University graduate, sometime between 1873 and 1906. The collection was received at the Yale Peabody Museum on April 21, 1906.
Human remains representing, at least, one individual have been identified. No associated funerary objects are present. Based on a letter received from the collectors, the collection was removed from near Fort Bayard in Grant County by Harvey B. McClure and Major A.B. Smith some time prior to November 13, 1919. The collection was received at the Yale Peabody Museum on February 24, 1920.
Human remains representing, at least, 14 individuals have been identified. No associated funerary objects are present. The collection was removed from the C-F ranch site in the Mangas Valley in Grant County in 1938 by John Rodman Paul, professor at the Yale School of Medicine. An exact location for this provenience is not known. The collection was received at the Yale Peabody Museum in January 1940.
Human remains representing, at least, one individual have been identified. No associated funerary objects are present. The collection was removed from the Thompson Ruin in the Mangas Valley in Grant County in 1938 by John Rodman Paul, professor at the Yale School of Medicine. The collection was received at the Yale Peabody Museum in January 1940.
Human remains representing, at least, one individual have been identified. No associated funerary objects are present. The collection was removed from the Corral Ruin within proximity to Tyrone in Grant County in 1938 by John Rodman Paul, professor at the Yale School of Medicine. The collection was received at the Yale Peabody Museum in January 1940.
Human remains representing, at least, seven individuals have been identified. No associated funerary objects are present. The collection was removed from the region of the Mangas Valley in Grant County in 1938 by John Rodman Paul, professor at the Yale School of Medicine. The collection was received at the Yale Peabody Museum in January 1940.
Human remains representing, at least, one individual have been identified. No associated funerary objects are present. The collection was removed from Saddle Rock Ruin in 1938 by John Rodman Paul, professor at the Yale School of Medicine. The collection was received at the Yale Peabody Museum in January 1940.
Human remains representing, at least, two individuals have been identified. The seven associated funerary objects are one ceramic ladle, four ceramic sherds, one lot of ceramic sherds, and one partially mended ceramic vessel. The collection was removed by Carmen Pagano in 1956 from a locale referred to as Canyon Sita, near Albuquerque. An exact provenience is unknown but is likely to be a Bernalillo County location of either Cañoncito, in the East Mountain area, or the land of the To'hajiilee Navajo Chapter, formerly named the Cañoncito Band of Navajos. The collection was received at the Yale Peabody Museum on June 19, 1956.
Human remains representing, at least, one individual have been identified. The 10 associated funerary objects are nine lots of ceramic sherds and one fragment of oxidized iron. The collection was removed by Carmen Pagano in 1956 from Golden, a census-designated locale in Santa Fe County. The collection was received at the Yale Peabody Museum on June 19, 1956.
Cultural Affiliation
Based on the information available and the results of consultation, cultural affiliation is clearly identified by the information available about the human remains and associated funerary objects described in this notice.
Determinations
The Yale Peabody Museum has determined that:
The human remains described in this notice represent the physical
(
printed page 66718)
remains of 36 individuals of Native American ancestry.
The 20 objects described in this notice are reasonably believed to have been placed intentionally with or near individual human remains at the time of death or later as part of the death rite or ceremony.
There is a connection between the human remains and associated funerary objects described in this notice and the Hopi Tribe of Arizona; Navajo Nation, Arizona, New Mexico, & Utah; Ohkay Owingeh, New Mexico; Pueblo of Acoma, New Mexico; Pueblo of Cochiti, New Mexico; Pueblo of Isleta, New Mexico; Pueblo of Jemez, New Mexico; Pueblo of Laguna, New Mexico; Pueblo of Nambe, New Mexico; Pueblo of Picuris, New Mexico; Pueblo of Pojoaque, New Mexico; Pueblo of San Felipe, New Mexico; Pueblo of San Ildefonso, New Mexico; Pueblo of Sandia, New Mexico; Pueblo of Santa Ana, New Mexico; Pueblo of Santa Clara, New Mexico; Pueblo of Taos, New Mexico; Pueblo of Tesuque, New Mexico; Pueblo of Zia, New Mexico; Santo Domingo Pueblo; Ysleta del Sur Pueblo; and the Zuni Tribe of the Zuni Reservation, New Mexico.

Repatriation of the human remains and associated funerary objects described in this notice to a requestor may occur on or after November 23, 2026. In accordance with the Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act (NAGPRA), the University of Arkansas Museum has completed an inventory of human remains and associated funerary objects and has determined that there is a cultural affiliation between the human remains and associated funerary objects and Indian Tribes or Native Hawaiian organizations in this notice.
DATES:
Repatriation of the human remains and associated funerary objects in this notice may occur on or after November 23, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
Send written requests for repatriation of the human remains and associated funerary objects in this notice to Dr. Mary Suter, Curator of Collections, The University of Arkansas Museum, University of Arkansas, Fayetteville, AR 72701, email

.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
This notice is published as part of the National Park Service's administrative responsibilities under NAGPRA. The determinations in this notice are the sole responsibility of the University of Arkansas Museum, and additional information on the determinations in this notice, including the results of consultation, can be found in its inventory or related records. The National Park Service is not responsible for the determinations in this notice.
Abstract of Information Available
In 1962, Charles McGimsey of the University of Arkansas undertook archaeological research at the Mineral Springs site (3HO1) on the Millwood Reservoir, Howard County, AR. Artifacts indicate a Fourche Maline phase with a Caddoan Mississippian occupation of the site from 500 BC to the Contact Period. Burials were excavated during legally authorized excavations by the University of Arkansas Museum. The collection is located at the University of Arkansas Museum, University of Arkansas, Fayetteville, AR. There are no known hazardous substances used to treat any of the human remains or associated funerary objects. The 15 associated funerary objects are two pieces of glass, five pieces of clay, and eight flakes.
In 1961, Michael P. Hoffman of the University of Arkansas undertook archaeological research at the Bell site (3HO11) on the Millwood Reservoir, Howard County, AR. Artifacts indicate a late Fourche Maline phase with a Caddoan Mississippian occupation of the site from 500 BC to the Contact Period. Burials were excavated during legally authorized excavations by the University of Arkansas Museum. The collection is located at the University of Arkansas Museum, University of Arkansas, Fayetteville, AR. Human remains representing, at least, six individuals have been identified. No known individuals were identified. There are no known hazardous substances used to treat any of the human remains or associated funerary objects. The 194 associated funerary objects are 47 bones, four charcoal, 10 daub, two flakes, one pipe stem, 30 shells, and 100 sherds.
In the early 1960s, under the direction of James Scholtz, the University of Arkansas undertook archaeological research at the White Cliffs site (3LR12) on the Millwood Reservoir, Little River County, AR. Artifacts indicate an early Caddoan Mississippian occupation of the site from A.D. 900 to 1200. Burials were excavated during legally authorized excavations by the University of Arkansas Museum. The collection is located at the University of Arkansas Museum, University of Arkansas, Fayetteville, AR. There are no known hazardous substances used to treat any of the human remains or associated funerary objects. The 2,215 associated funerary objects are 37 bones, 656 flakes, 305 lithic samples, three shells, one shell casing (ammunition), and 1,213 sherds.
In the early 1960s, under the direction of Charles McGimsey, the University of Arkansas Museum undertook archaeological research at the Old Martin Place site (3LR49) on the Millwood Reservoir, Little River County, AR. Artifacts indicate a Fourche Maline phase with a Caddoan Mississippian occupation of the site from 500 to the Contact Period. Burials were excavated during legally authorized excavations by the University of Arkansas Museum. The collection is located at the University of Arkansas Museum, University of Arkansas, Fayetteville, AR. There are no known hazardous substances used to treat any of the human remains or associated funerary objects. The 804 associated funerary objects are nine antlers, five antler artifacts, 10 bone awls, 639 bones, two daub, one fish hook, 12 shells, 112 sherds, 13 stones, and one wood.
In the early 1960s, Michael P. Hoffman of the University of Arkansas Museum undertook archaeological research at the Millers Crossing site (3SV10) on the Millwood Reservoir, Sevier County, AR. Artifacts indicate an early Caddoan Mississippian occupation of the site from A.D. 900 to 1200. Burials were excavated during legally authorized excavations by the University of Arkansas Museum. The collection is located at the University of Arkansas Museum, University of Arkansas, Fayetteville, AR. There are no known hazardous substances used to treat any of the human remains or associated funerary objects. The seven associated funerary objects are one pigment, two metal, one galena, two jars, and one bowl.
In the early 1980s, human remains representing, at minimum, one individual were removed from the Millers Crossing site (3SV10) on Millwood Reservoir, Sevier County, AR. The human remains and associated funerary object were donated to the University of Arkansas by a private donor. Artifacts indicate an early Caddoan Mississippian occupation of the site from A.D. 900 to 1200. The collection is located at the University of Arkansas Museum, University of Arkansas, Fayetteville, AR. There are no known hazardous substances used to treat any of the human remains or associated funerary objects. No known individuals were identified. The one associated funerary object is one sherd.
In the early 1960s, Michael P. Hoffman of the University of Arkansas undertook archaeological research at the Graves Chapel site (3SV15) on the Millwood Reservoir, Sevier Co., AR. Artifacts indicate a late Archaic period (3000-650 BC) and Late Woodland (A.D. 500-900) to Early Caddoan Mississippian (A.D. 900-1200) components of the site. Burials were excavated during legally authorized excavations by the University of Arkansas Museum. The collection is located at the University of Arkansas Museum, University of Arkansas, Fayetteville, AR. There are no known hazardous substances used to treat any of the human remains or associated funerary objects. The 154 associated funerary objects are 18 flakes, 96 bones, 27 shells, two ground stones, three cores, and eight sherds.
In the early 1960s, human remains representing, at minimum, one individual were removed from the Hutt
(
printed page 66721)
site (3HE3) on Millwood Reservoir, Hempstead County, AR. Burials were excavated during legally authorized excavations by the University of Arkansas Museum. Artifacts indicate an early Caddoan Mississippian occupation of the site from A.D. 900 to 1200. The collection is located at the University of Arkansas Museum, University of Arkansas, Fayetteville, AR. There are no known hazardous substances used to treat any of the human remains or associated funerary objects. No known individuals were identified. There are no associated funerary objects.
Cultural Affiliation
Based on the information available and the results of consultation, cultural affiliation with the Caddo Nation of Oklahoma is clearly identified by the information available about the associated funerary objects described in this notice.
Determinations
The University of Arkansas Museum has determined that:
The human remains described in this notice represent the physical remains of eight individuals of Native American ancestry.
The 3,390 objects described in this notice are reasonably believed to have been placed intentionally with or near individual human remains at the time of death or later as part of the death rite or ceremony.
There is a connection between the human remains and associated funerary objects described in this notice and the Caddo Nation of Oklahoma.
Requests for Repatriation
Written requests for repatriation of the human remains and associated funerary objects in this notice must be sent to the authorized representative identified in this notice under
ADDRESSES
. Requests for repatriation may be submitted by:
1. Any one or more of the Indian Tribes or Native Hawaiian organizations identified in this notice.
2. Any lineal descendant, Indian Tribe, or Native Hawaiian organization not identified in this notice who shows, by a preponderance of the evidence, that the requestor is a lineal descendant or an Indian Tribe or Native Hawaiian organization with cultural affiliation.
Repatriation of the human remains and associated funerary objects described in this notice to a requestor may occur on or after November 23, 2026. If competing requests for repatriation are received, the University of Arkansas Museum must determine the most appropriate requestor prior to repatriation. Requests for joint repatriation of the human remains and associated funerary objects are considered a single request and not competing requests. The University of Arkansas Museum is responsible for sending a copy of this notice to the Indian Tribes and Native Hawaiian organizations identified in this notice and any other consulting parties.
Authority:
Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act,
25 U.S.C. 3003
, and the implementing regulations,
43 CFR 10.10
.
Dated: October 15, 2026.

Manager, National NAGPRA Program.
